exp.0:1:
This verse says that God, after speaking to his people in many ways in the past, has now spoken to us through his Son. "Last days" means the final times, the last stage of God's plan. "Heir of all things" means that the Son receives everything as his own. And the universe was made through him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. They may have been tempted to return to the old ways. He shows them that Jesus is greater than the prophets and the angels, because he is God's final and complete word.

For today: if you want to know what God is like, look to Jesus. Read about him carefully in the Gospels, and let his voice guide your daily decisions.
exp.0:8:
He says the Son loved what is right and hated what is wrong. Therefore God, who is his God, anointed him (chose him and honored him) with the oil of gladness, that is, with joy and honor, above his companions. That word can refer to other kings or to those who share his kingdom with him; interpreters understand it in different ways.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, quotes Psalm 45:6-7. He wants to show that Jesus is greater than the angels. God calls the angels servants, but he calls the Son God and gives him an eternal throne. His reign is just because he loves righteousness.

For today: ask God that your heart may love what is good and reject what is evil, as Jesus did. Today, choose one small decision where you can act with honesty, even if it costs you. That is where a life of true joy begins.
exp.0:9:
It says that the Lord was the one who, in the beginning, laid the foundations of the earth, and that the heavens are the works of his hands. The word "laid" means that you set in place or established a firm base. The phrase "in the beginning" points to the origin of creation.

The writer of Hebrews is showing that Jesus, the Son, is superior to the angels. Here he quotes Psalm 102:25-27, a psalm addressed to God, and applies it to the Son. In this way he affirms that Christ is not a creature, but took part in creation. Some scholars debate how the psalm was applied, but the general meaning in the letter is clear: the Son is Creator and is eternal.

For today: if Christ made all things and remains when everything changes, you can trust him in the midst of uncertainty. When you feel that nothing is secure, pray and entrust your worries to the One who sustains the universe and does not change.
exp.0:12:
This verse asks a rhetorical question: to which of the angels did God ever say, "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet?" The answer is: to none of them. The place at the right hand stands for honor and authority. The footstool is the low seat where the feet rest; placing enemies under the feet speaks of complete victory.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, quotes Psalm 110:1. He wants to show believers of Jewish background that Jesus is superior to the angels. The angels serve, but only the Son is invited to reign with God.

For today: when you feel that evil is advancing or that your problems are too big, remember that Christ already reigns and his final victory is secured. You can rest and obey with hope, without fear.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that the angels are spirits who serve God. He sends them to help those who will receive salvation as their inheritance. The word "ministering" here means serving or helping. Salvation in this verse refers to being saved, not just to physical health. And those who will receive what God promised are the heirs.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, compares Jesus with the angels. The angels are admirable, but they are servants. Jesus, by contrast, is the Son, and God invited him to sit at his right hand. In this way the author shows that Christ is superior and worthy of complete trust.

For today: you can rest knowing that God cares for you in ways you do not see. You do not need to worship angels or seek them out; your trust should be in Jesus. Today, thank God for his care and serve others with humility, as the angels do.
exp.1:2:
This verse asks a serious question: if we ignore or neglect such a great salvation, how will we escape judgment? Here "salvation" is the word for the rescue God offers, and "neglect" means to give it little importance. This salvation was first announced by the Lord Jesus and then confirmed to the readers by those who heard him directly.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who may have been growing weary or drifting away. He compares the message that came through angels, which was enforced firmly, with the message of the Son, which is even greater. That is why his warning is stronger.

For today: do not take your faith for granted. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and pray, so that you do not slowly drift away from what God has given you.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that God himself backed up the message of salvation given by the first witnesses. He did this with signs (deeds that point to something beyond themselves), with miracles (works of power), and with wonders (things that cause amazement). He also did it with gifts of the Holy Spirit, that is, gifts that he distributed as he willed.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were in danger of neglecting their faith. He reminds them that the salvation announced by Jesus was confirmed by those who heard him, and that God himself gave testimony that this message is true. For that reason it should not be taken lightly.

Today we can take the gospel seriously and not treat it as something already known. God has backed it up with firmness, so it is worth listening to it carefully, obeying it, and giving thanks for the gifts that he gives his people to serve others.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that Jesus came to free the people who spent their whole lives held captive by the fear of dying. That fear kept them as if they were slaves.

Context: the author of Hebrews does not name himself, and we cannot be certain who he was. He writes to show that Jesus truly became human, sharing in flesh and blood. By dying, he defeated the devil, who held power over death. In this way, Jesus identified himself with us in order to rescue us.

For today: if the fear of death or of the future weighs on you, you can bring it to Jesus in prayer. He knows human suffering and has already overcome death. Remembering his resurrection can bring you peace, so that you live with more freedom and confidence, and not with anguish.
exp.2:1:
It says that Jesus was faithful to God the Father, who appointed him to his mission, just as Moses was faithful in all of God's house. The people of God are what the "house" refers to.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who may have been tempted to give up or turn back. To encourage them, he compares Jesus with Moses, whom they greatly respected. He acknowledges Moses' faithfulness, but he prepares the way to show that Christ is superior.

Today we can learn that faithfulness matters to God. Jesus was faithful to the end, and that gives us confidence to follow him. We can ask him for help to be faithful in what he has entrusted to us, even if it seems small: our family, our work, or our service in the church.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that God was displeased with that generation of Israel. Being angry with them means that he was indignant and grew angry with them. Their hearts went astray, wandering from one place to another without direction. And although they saw God's works, they did not come to know his ways, that is, they did not learn to live as he teaches.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and presents God speaking about the people who came out of Egypt. For forty years in the desert they doubted and complained, even while witnessing miracles. The writer uses this to warn believers: do not repeat that same unbelief.

For today: it is not enough to see or hear what God does; we must respond to him with trust and obedience. When you feel your heart drifting or hardening, stop, pray, and ask God to teach you his ways.
exp.2:15:
This verse reminds us that some of the people God brought out of Egypt, although they heard his voice, provoked him, that is, they offended him by rebelling against him. Some translations read it as a question: "Who were those who, having heard, provoked him? Were they not all those who came out of Egypt?" The text allows both readings.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, quotes Psalm 95 and recalls the rebellion of the people in the wilderness, as told in Numbers 14. He writes to believers tempted to abandon their faith, and he warns them with an example from Israel's history.

For today: having seen God's work is not enough if we stop trusting and obeying. Today, when you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word, respond with humility and obedience instead of putting it off or hardening your heart.
exp.2:16:
This verse asks a question in order to answer it right away: with whom was God angry for forty years? With those who sinned, that is, those whose bodies fell dead in the wilderness.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers who were tempted to lose heart. He cites Psalm 95 and reminds his readers of the people of Israel who left Egypt, distrusted God, and died in the wilderness before entering the promised land. He uses this as a warning to his readers.

For today: when God speaks to you through his Word, do not delay your response or let your heart grow hard little by little. Trust him and obey him today, even when the road is long or difficult.
exp.3:11:
The explanation says that the word of God is not dead or weak, but living and powerful. It is sharper than any two-edged sword and reaches to the deepest part of a person. The phrase about piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, is a way of speaking about reaching the most inner parts of a person. It also speaks of discerning, that is, judging, the thoughts and intents of the heart.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers. He warns them not to repeat the disobedience of Israel in the wilderness, which lost the rest that was promised. The word of God is the voice that calls them to obey today.

For today: read the Bible with an open heart, letting God reveal your hidden motives. Ask Him to correct you with love and to help you obey.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that every high priest is chosen from among human beings themselves. His work is to represent the people before God and to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. The word "high priest" here means the chief priest, and the "gifts" are offerings or gifts brought to God.

The author of Hebrews is unknown; tradition has proposed several names, but there is no certainty. He writes to believers with a Jewish background, and he begins to explain how Jesus is the perfect priest. To do this, he first describes what a high priest did in Israel, and then he will show how Christ fulfills and surpasses that role.

For today: God wanted our mediator to be someone who understands human weakness. When you feel far from God or ashamed of your failures, remember that you can draw near to Him with confidence, because Jesus knows what we live through and intercedes for you.
exp.4:2:
The explanation says that the human high priest, being full of weakness, had to present offerings for his own sins just as he did for the sins of the people.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows with certainty who he was) explains how the priesthood of Israel worked. He wants his readers to understand that the priest was someone like them, who could sympathize with the weak. This prepares the contrast with Christ, whom he presents shortly afterward as the High Priest called by God.

For today: recognizing our own weakness makes us more humble and compassionate toward others. If we have been called to guide or correct someone, let us do so remembering that we too need the forgiveness and grace of God.
exp.4:3:
No one takes this honor on himself. That position of high priest is received only from the one whom God calls, as happened with Aaron. Here "honor" means an office of dignity and service before God, not simple praise.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) explains what a high priest was: a weak man, able to understand those who had gone astray, who offered sacrifices also for his own sins. Then he shows that Christ fulfills this: he did not appoint himself, but the Father called him. In this way the theme of Jesus as the eternal priest is prepared.

For today: do not seek positions or recognition out of ambition. Ask God what he is calling you to, serve with humility, and trust that he opens doors in his own time.
exp.4:8:
It says that Jesus, after being made perfect, that is, brought to his goal or completed in his work, became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey him. Here "salvation" means rescue from sin and its consequences, not only well-being of the body. Being made perfect does not mean that Jesus had any flaws, but that he completed the path the Father had given him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who are weary and full of doubts. He has just shown Jesus as the Son who suffered and learned obedience. Now he says that this path of suffering opened salvation for others, and he presents him as high priest in the manner of Melchizedek.

For today: obedience to Christ is not a burden to earn heaven, but the confident response to the One who already walked the hard road for us. Today you can choose one concrete step of obedience, even if it costs you, trusting that he understands you.
exp.4:9:
He says that God himself appointed Jesus as high priest, and that his priesthood follows the order of Melchisedec. This means that he does not belong to the line of priests descended from Aaron, but to a different kind of priesthood, one that is unique and older.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers who had stopped growing in their spiritual life. He has just said that Jesus learned obedience through suffering. Now he mentions Melchisedec, a king and priest who appears in Genesis 14, and says there is much to explain, but his readers have become slow to understand.

For today: if Jesus is our high priest appointed by God, we can draw near to him with confidence in prayer. And it is worth asking ourselves whether we are still growing, or whether we are still content with milk when God wants to give us solid food.
exp.4:11:
It says that, given how long they had been believers, they should already be teaching others. Yet they once again needed someone to explain to them the most basic things of God's word. They had come to need the simple teaching of the faith, the kind suited to someone just starting out, and not the solid food meant for the mature. The first lessons, the elementary basics, are what they had gone back to needing.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He was speaking about Jesus as high priest according to the order of Melchizedek, but he pauses to correct them lovingly: not because they lacked ability, but because they had become slow to listen and to grow.

For today: do not settle for what you learned at the beginning. Set aside a fixed time each week to study the Bible more deeply, and aim to put what you learn into practice, because that is how a person matures.
exp.5:1:
This verse continues a list of basic teachings of the Christian faith: the baptisms (in the plural), the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. Laying on of hands means placing hands on someone, a gesture that in the Bible was used to bless, to pray for a person, or to set someone apart for a service. It is not known with certainty which baptisms are meant; some think of different kinds of washing or purification, or of Christian baptism compared with other washings.

The author of Hebrews (we do not know for certain who he was) writes to believers who had stopped growing. He tells them that they already have the foundations and that it is time to grow into maturity, without starting over from the beginning.

For today: do not settle for the basics of your faith. Be thankful for the foundations, but keep learning, reading the Bible, and putting into practice what you understand, so that you grow every day.
exp.5:5:
It says that it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who, after knowing so closely the blessings of God, have fallen away. The idea of falling away speaks of turning away from faith. To treat Christ with contempt, as if his sacrifice were worth nothing, is what the phrase about crucifying the Son of God again means. Public shame or insult is what the idea of disgrace before others refers to.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to Jewish believers who may have felt pressure to abandon Christ. He warns them firmly and then encourages them. Christians interpret this passage in various ways: some see a warning about losing salvation, others see a description of those who never truly believed.

Today it invites us to take our faith seriously and not treat it with indifference. If you feel yourself drifting away, return to Christ soon with humility, and nurture your spiritual life through prayer and community.
exp.5:6:
It says that the earth which soaks up the rain that falls on it many times, and which yields a good crop for those who work it, receives God's blessing.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were at risk of drifting away from the faith. Earlier he spoke of those who tasted God's blessings and then let them go. Now he uses the picture of a field: the same rain falls on all the ground, but the result is different. Those who interpret this passage disagree about the fate of those who fall away, but all agree that it is a serious warning.

Today, it is not enough to hear the Word many times. God looks for fruit: love, obedience, and perseverance. Ask yourself what you have done with what you have already received, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that God is righteous and does not forget what you have done. He remembers your work and the labor of love you showed toward his name, by helping the saints, that is, the believers, and by continuing to help them still.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were tired and tempted to give up. First he gives them a serious warning, but then he calls them dear friends and tells them he expects better things from them. This verse encourages them: their service has value to God. Then he invites them to keep going steadily to the end, with faith and patience.

For today: do not underestimate simple, steady service, such as visiting someone who is sick, helping a brother or sister, or serving in your church without applause. God sees it and remembers it. Be encouraged to keep serving with love, without growing weary.
exp.5:10:
It says that the author wants each believer to keep showing the same earnest effort, the same eagerness, that they have already shown, and to keep doing so to the very end. The goal is that hope be fully fulfilled, that is, that it become complete certainty.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, has just issued a stern warning about the danger of drifting away. Now he speaks with tenderness, calling them dear friends. He acknowledges their service to the saints and tells them that God does not forget that love. He asks them not to slacken, because faith is tested over time.

For today: do not lose heart if your service seems to bear no fruit. Choose one concrete act of love, such as visiting, helping, or praying for someone, and keep it up faithfully, trusting that God sees and does not forget your work.
exp.5:11:
Hebrews 6:12 tells us not to become lazy, meaning sluggish or idle in the life of faith. Instead, we should imitate those who, trusting God and waiting with patience, receive what God has promised. The word "inherit" means they receive it as a gift, not as a wage.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, is writing to Christians who had served with love but could grow weary. He has just encouraged them to keep the same diligence until the end. Then he points to Abraham, to whom God made a sure promise.

For today: when you feel weariness in your faith, do not give up. Choose one simple practice, such as praying each day or serving someone, and keep at it, trusting that God keeps what he promises.
exp.5:12:
This verse says that when God made a promise to Abraham, He swore by Himself, because there was no one greater than Him to swear by. Making a promise is one thing, and swearing is confirming with a solemn commitment that one is telling the truth and will keep it.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who were growing weary in their faith. He asks them not to be lazy, but to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. He holds up Abraham as an example, reminding them that God confirmed His word with an oath, as seen in Genesis 22.

For today: when the waiting becomes long and you begin to doubt, remember that God does not only promise, but backs His word with His own character. You can rest in that and keep trusting with patience, one day at a time, praying and obeying.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that people, when they want to make sure something is true, swear by someone greater than themselves, such as God or a higher authority. Disputes are the arguments or disagreements between people. Giving assurance is what makes an oath a guarantee. In other words, an oath puts an end to arguments because it guarantees that what was said is true.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who needed to stay firm. He has just recalled that God promised Abraham blessing and descendants. He uses the human custom of oaths to explain that God, in swearing, wanted to give even greater assurance to his promise.

For today: when you doubt or feel insecure, remember that God not only promises, but has bound himself to his word in a solemn way. You can rely on that and pray with confidence, waiting patiently as Abraham did.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that the hope we have in God is like an anchor for the soul: sure and firm. The veil was the curtain of the temple that separated the Most Holy Place, where God's presence was. The high priest is the one who entered there once a year, and the forerunner is the one who goes ahead to open the way.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired and tempted to give up. He reminds them that God made a promise and confirmed it with an oath. Two things that do not change, God's promise and his oath, give strong comfort. This hope reaches all the way into God's presence, because Jesus has already entered there for us as high priest.

For today: when storms come, such as sickness, fear, or uncertainty, do not lean on your feelings, which change. Pray and remember a specific promise of God, and rest in the fact that Jesus is already where you long to arrive.
exp.6:0:
This verse presents Melchisedec as king of Salem and priest of the Most High God. When Abraham was returning from defeating the kings who had taken his nephew Lot, Melchisedec went out to meet him and blessed him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He returns to the account in Genesis 14 to show that Christ is a priest of an order different from and superior to that of Aaron. Melchisedec appears suddenly in the story, and that is why he is used as a figure who points to Jesus.

For today: after a victory or an achievement, recognize that God is the one who sustains you. Receive the blessing of others with humility, and give thanks to God, our High Priest.
exp.6:1:
Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth part of everything he had recovered. The text explains the meaning of his name: "King of righteousness." He was also king of Salem, which means "King of peace."

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a priest greater than the priests of the temple. To do this, he uses Melchizedek, who appears briefly in Genesis 14. The meanings of his name and of his city point to what Christ brings.

For today: Jesus unites righteousness and peace. If you have failed and feel restless, come to Him with confidence. And seek to live justly and peacefully with those around you.
exp.6:3:
Consider how great Melchizedek was, to whom even Abraham, the patriarch and father of the people of Israel, gave a tenth of the best of the spoils of war.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to their former faith. He wants to show that Jesus is superior to the priesthood of Levi. He uses Melchizedek, who blessed Abraham, to point out that this priesthood is earlier and greater, and that it points to Christ.

For today: Jesús is greater than any tradition or religious figure we might trust in. Today we can give him first place, and give with gratitude, recognizing that everything we have comes from God.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that the priests descended from Levi had a command in the law of Moses: to collect tithes from the people of Israel. In other words, they took a tenth from their own brothers, who were also descendants of Abraham.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, a priest after the manner of Melchizedek, is superior to the Levitical priesthood. First he points out that the Levites collected tithes by command of the law. Later he will say that Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek, which shows the greatness of Melchizedek.

For today: value Jesus as your supreme priest. Instead of trusting in rituals or traditions, draw near to God with confidence through Christ, and pray each day knowing that he intercedes for you.
exp.6:5:
This verse speaks of Melchizedek. It says that he did not belong to the family of Levi, that is, he did not have Israel's priestly descent. Even so, he received tithes (a tenth part) from Abraham and blessed him, even though Abraham was the one who had received God's promises.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers with a Jewish background, and he wants to show that Christ is superior to the Levitical priesthood. He recalls the meeting in Genesis 14: Abraham gave tithes to Melchizedek and was blessed by him. The argument is that the priesthood of Melchizedek, to which Christ is compared, is of a higher order than that of Levi.

For today: we do not need human go-betweens to come to God, because Christ is our priest. We can approach Him with confidence, and respond to Him with gratitude, honoring Him with what we have and with our lives.
exp.6:7:
This verse compares two groups who receive tithes. On one side are the Levitical priests, who are mortal men: they collect the tithe, but then they die and others take their place. On the other side is Melchizedek, of whom Scripture bears witness that he lives, meaning that his death is not mentioned.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers of Jewish background, who were probably tempted to return to the old ways. He wants to show that Christ, a priest after the order of Melchizedek, is superior to the Levitical priesthood. Scholars debate whether Melchizedek literally lives or whether the point is only the silence of the account about his death (Genesis 14; Psalm 110:4).

For today: our hope does not depend on leaders who die and are replaced, but on Jesus, who lives forever. You can pray today with confidence, knowing that he intercedes for you.
exp.6:10:
This verse asks a question: if the priesthood of Levi, with its law and its sacrifices, could bring a person to perfection (that is, to a complete and true relationship with God, with sin truly dealt with), why did God announce another priest, after the order of Melchisedec and not of Aaron?

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He has just shown that Melchisedec is greater than Levi, because Abraham gave him a tenth. His point is that the Levitical priesthood was not enough, and that is why God promised another (Psalm 110:4).

For today: do not trust your efforts, rituals, or good behavior to make you right with God. Rest in Jesus, our high priest, who can truly give us full access to God.
exp.6:11:
Here "changed" means altered, and "change" means alteration. The author states that if the priesthood is changed, the law that depended on it must also be changed. The law and the Levitical priesthood were closely bound together.

The book of Hebrews was addressed to believers with a Jewish background. Its author is unknown. Its purpose is to show that Jesus, of the tribe of Judah and a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, is superior to the priesthood of Aaron. If God appointed a new priest, He also established a new way of drawing near to Him. Christians understand in different ways how far this change in the law extends.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus is our priest. We do not need to earn God's favor through rituals. We can approach Him with confidence, through Christ.
exp.6:12:
He of whom these things are spoken, Jesus, the one Psalm 110 speaks about, belongs to a tribe other than the priestly one. The phrase "served at the altar" means that he served as priest at the altar. No member of the tribe of Judah had served there, because the law reserved that office for the tribe of Levi, and especially for the descendants of Aaron.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a superior priest. If the priesthood changed, the law that governed it changed as well. Jesus came from Judah, and so his priesthood is not based on family inheritance but on the order of Melchizedek.

For today: you do not need merit, lineage, or rituals to come near to God. Jesus, our priest, opens the way for you. Go to him with confidence in prayer.
exp.6:17:
The explanation says that the earlier commandment, that is, the law that organized the Levitical priesthood, is set aside or put to one side. The reason is that it was weak and could not accomplish what it promised. The word the verse uses for this setting aside means that it is cancelled or no longer has effect.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whom scholars debate, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have wanted to return to the old ways. He has just shown that Jesus is a priest in the order of Melchizedek, not by human descent. For that reason he explains that the earlier system could not bring people into a full relationship with God, and that Christ brings a better hope.

For today: do not trust your religious efforts, routines, or merits to make you feel accepted by God. Draw near to Him with confidence, resting on Jesus, who lives forever and opens the way for us.
exp.6:20:
This verse compares the priests of the Old Testament with Jesus. The Levites became priests without God making an oath. Jesus, however, was made priest with an oath. God himself said to him: "The Lord swore, and will not change his mind: You are a priest forever." "Forever" means for all time, and "will not change his mind" means that God will not change his purpose.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background, who were probably tempted to return to the law and its sacrifices. He quotes Psalm 110:4 to show that the priesthood of Jesus is superior: it is backed by God's solemn promise and does not depend on a family line. Who wrote the letter is not known with certainty.

For today: your relationship with God rests on a Priest whom God himself confirmed with an oath. When you doubt your forgiveness, remember that his commitment does not change. Draw near to God with confidence, relying on Jesus and not on your performance.
exp.6:26:
This verse says that Jesus, our high priest, does not need to offer sacrifices every day as the other priests did. They first offered for their own sins and then for the sins of the people. Jesus, by contrast, did it once, when he offered himself.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Christ is superior to the priests of the law. Those priests were weak and sinful men; Jesus is holy, without sin, and his sacrifice is complete and does not need to be repeated.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or carry guilt that has already been forgiven. You can draw near to God with confidence, because Jesus has already paid for everything. Rest in his finished work and respond with gratitude and obedience.
exp.6:27:
This verse compares two kinds of priests. The law of Moses appointed men as high priests who were weak, with flaws and sins. But the word of the oath, which God spoke after the law (referring to Psalm 110:4), appoints the Son as priest. He was made complete and without fault forever, and his priesthood never ends.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to the system of priests and sacrifices. He shows them that Jesus is superior, because he does not need to offer sacrifices for his own sins, and his one offering was enough forever.

Today we can rest in the fact that our relationship with God does not depend on our own perfection or on that of any human leader. Jesus is a faithful and permanent priest. You can approach God with confidence, speaking to him in prayer, even when you feel weak.
exp.7:2:
Every high priest, the verse says, is appointed to present gifts and sacrifices to God. Gifts here means offerings or presents. So if Jesus is our High Priest, he also had to have something to offer.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, wrote to Christians of Jewish background who knew the system of sacrifices well. He explains that Jesus serves in the heavenly sanctuary, not in the earthly temple. Later in the letter, it makes clear that what Christ offered was his own life.

For today: you do not have to draw near to God on the strength of your own merits or try to make up for your failures. Jesus has already offered what was needed. You can pray with confidence and gratitude, knowing that you have a High Priest who represents you before God.
exp.7:3:
It says that if Jesus were here on earth, he would not even be a priest, because there are already priests who offer the gifts according to the law of Moses. The word "gifts" here means the offerings or gifts that were brought to God. Jesus did not belong to the tribe of Levi, which was the tribe of the priests.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus serves in a heavenly sanctuary, not in the earthly temple. His priesthood is different and superior, and so it does not compete with the old system.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus intercedes for us in God's presence. We do not need to seek other intermediaries or depend on rituals to draw near. We can pray with confidence, knowing that our High Priest understands us and welcomes us.
exp.7:5:
It says that Jesus now has a ministry far more excellent than that of the ancient priests. The reason is that he is the mediator, that is, the one who brings God and people together, of a better covenant. A covenant is a solemn commitment of God to his people. This new covenant rests on better promises.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background, perhaps tempted to return to the old customs. He has just said that the priests of the temple served as a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. Now he shows that Christ is the reality. Soon he will quote Jeremiah's promise about a new covenant.

For today: you do not have to approach God in fear or trying to earn his favor. Jesus is your mediator, and God's promises rest on him. Today you can pray with confidence, knowing that he presents you before the Father.
exp.8:1:
This verse describes the first part of the tabernacle, the holy tent that Israel used in the wilderness. In it were the lampstand, the table, and the bread that was set out before God. This first space was called the Sanctuary, or the Holy Place.

The writer of Hebrews addresses believers of Jewish background and compares the first covenant with the new one. Before showing that Christ fulfills everything, he describes the tabernacle in detail. We do not know for certain who wrote the letter, but his purpose is clear: to show that Jesus is better than the ancient rites.

For today: the lamps, the table, and the bread point to light, fellowship, and provision. Today we can draw near to God through Christ, without complicated rituals. Take a moment today to pray with confidence, giving thanks that you have access to Him.
exp.8:3:
This passage describes the Most Holy Place. It had a golden censer (some think this refers to the altar of incense). Also there was the ark of the covenant, covered with gold. Inside it was a golden jar with manna, Aaron's rod that budded (put out shoots), and the tables of the law.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He describes the ancient tabernacle to show that Christ brings something better. These objects reminded the people of God's care, his authority, and his law.

For today: remember how God has sustained you, as he did with the manna. And since Christ opened the way to God, you can draw near to him with confidence in prayer.
exp.8:4:
This verse describes the upper part of the ark of the covenant. Above it were the cherubims of glory, figures of angelic beings, whose wings covered the mercy seat, that is, the golden lid where the blood was sprinkled for forgiveness. The author says that he cannot now speak in detail about all these things.

The book of Hebrews was written by an author who is not named; tradition has proposed several names, but there is no certainty. It is written to believers with a Jewish background to show them that Christ is greater than the old worship. Here the author goes over the objects of the tabernacle to prepare his explanation: the high priest entered alone only once a year, while Christ opened the way forever.

For today: the mercy seat was the place where God met his people through the blood. Today we can draw near to God with confidence, not because of our merits, but because of Christ. If you feel far from God, pray today and come to him with simplicity.
exp.8:6:
Hebrews 9:7 says that only the high priest entered the second place, the Most Holy Place, and he did so only once a year. He never went in without blood. He offered it first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people committed in ignorance, that is, sins committed without their realizing it or without evil intent.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, describes the Old Testament tabernacle. This refers to the Day of Atonement, according to Leviticus 16. He wants to show believers with a Jewish background that this system had limits: access to God was restricted and had to be repeated every year.

For today: God does not take sin lightly, but He also does not keep us far away. You can approach Him with gratitude and confidence, remembering that Christ opened the way with his own blood.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that the tabernacle and its rituals were a picture, that is, an image or example, of that time before Christ. The gifts were the offerings, and the sacrifices were the animals brought. None of it could make the worshiper complete in regard to the conscience, that is, it could not cleanse the inside or take away the guilt of the heart.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that the tabernacle system pointed to something greater. He explains this so that they do not turn back, for in Christ they have what those rites only foretold.

For today: if your conscience accuses you of past failures, do not try to quiet it with your own efforts or rituals. Bring it to Christ, who can truly cleanse the heart, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that Christ did not enter the holy place with the blood of animals, as the ancient priests did, but with his own blood. He did it once for all, meaning in a definitive way, and so obtained eternal redemption. "Redemption" means rescue or deliverance. The "holy place" refers to the innermost sanctuary, where the blood was presented before God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Christ is superior to the priesthood and the sacrifices of the old covenant. Those rites were temporary, lasting until a time of setting things right, and they pointed toward something better.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through repeated efforts. You can rest in what Christ has already done and draw near to God with confidence, thankful and ready to serve him.
exp.8:12:
This verse speaks of the sacrifices of the Old Testament. The blood of bulls and male goats, and the ashes of a young cow sprinkled on those who were "unclean" (people who, according to the law, could not draw near to God), set them apart for God and cleansed them on the outside, in the ceremonial sense. The phrase "sanctifies for the purifying of the flesh" shows that this effect was external.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He wants to show them that the old was real but limited. This verse sets up a comparison: if that cleansed on the outside, the next verse says how much more the blood of Christ will do, cleansing from within.

For today: you do not have to strive to earn forgiveness through rituals or merits. Draw near to God with confidence, because Christ can cleanse your conscience from guilt and give you freedom to serve him.
exp.8:17:
This verse says that even the first covenant, the one God made with Israel through Moses, did not begin without blood.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has been explaining that a will requires the death of the one who made it. With this he prepares the way to show that Christ, by his blood, inaugurated a new and better covenant. The verses that follow recall when Moses sprinkled blood on the book and on the people.

For today: our forgiveness does not depend on our efforts, but on Christ's giving of himself. You can draw near to God with gratitude and confidence, without trying to earn what has already been paid for at such great cost.
exp.8:18:
Here the author recalls that Moses read to the people all the commandments of the law. Then he took the blood of calves and male goats, mixed it with water, and used red wool and hyssop, a small plant used for sprinkling. With these he sprinkled the book of the law and all the people.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the first covenant, made at Sinai (Exodus 24), was sealed with blood. In this way he prepares his argument: if that covenant required blood, the new covenant is confirmed with the blood of Christ.

For today: God draws near to us through a serious covenant, confirmed with blood. This reminds us that his forgiveness cost a great deal. We can receive it with gratitude and respond with sincere obedience, not out of fear, but out of love.
exp.8:20:
The verse says that Moses also sprinkled with blood the tabernacle, that is, the sacred tent where Israel worshiped God, and all the vessels of the ministry, that is, the utensils used in worship. Nothing was left unset apart for God through the blood.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He explains that the first covenant was inaugurated with blood, and that this pointed to something greater: the sacrifice of Christ. The verses that follow affirm this: without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, but the heavenly realities required a better sacrifice.

Today we can remember that drawing near to God never depended on our effort or our rituals. Christ has already paid the price. You can pray with confidence, without carrying guilt that He has already covered.
exp.8:23:
This verse says that Christ did not enter a temple built by human hands, which was only a copy or shadow of the true one. He entered heaven itself, to appear now before God on our behalf. The holy place where God was worshiped is the sanctuary, and the copy or shadow is what the temple was.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the temple's system of sacrifices pointed to something greater. The high priest entered the most holy place each year with blood that was not his own, but Jesus entered with his own sacrifice, once and for all.

Today you can rest knowing that Jesus is before God for you right now. You do not have to earn access to God through effort or rituals. When you feel guilty or far from God, pray with confidence, remembering that Christ has already opened the way and represents you.
exp.8:24:
It says that Jesus did not enter heaven to offer himself over and over. The high priest, who in the Jewish temple entered the most holy place every year, went in with blood that was not his own, the blood of animals. Christ, by contrast, offered his own blood.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to the temple rites. He shows them that Christ is superior: the old system was a shadow of the good things to come, and Christ entered heaven itself, before God.

For today: you do not need to earn forgiveness through repeated efforts or live in fear of not having done enough. Jesus' sacrifice was complete. You can draw near to God with confidence and gratitude, and respond with a life of love and obedience, not of fear.
exp.8:27:
It says that Christ was offered once to take away, bear, or carry the sins of many. The text speaks of two comings: the first, to bear sin; the second, without sin, meaning without having to deal with sin again, because it has already been resolved. Then he will be seen by those who are waiting for him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to Christians with a Jewish background. He compares Christ with the sacrifices in the temple, which were repeated. He reminds his readers that people die once and then comes judgment; in the same way, Christ was offered once. His work is complete and does not need to be repeated.

For today: if Christ has already dealt with sin, you can draw near to God with confidence, without trying to earn his forgiveness through effort. And while you wait for his return, live with hope and peace, not with fear.
exp.9:0:
The explanation says that the law of Moses was like a shadow: it showed from a distance the good things God would bring, but it was not the reality itself. For this reason, the sacrifices that were repeated every year could never make those who came to worship complete, fully cleansed before God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old customs. He explains to them that Christ fulfills what the law only announced. Here he begins to show that a sacrifice repeated again and again points to the need for one better and final.

For today: do not trust in religious routines or in your efforts to feel clean before God. Rest in what Christ has already done, and let that assurance lead you to draw near to Him with confidence and gratitude.
exp.9:2:
The explanation says that the sacrifices of the law, repeated every year, actually made sins be remembered. Each time the sacrifice was offered, the people were reminded that their sin was still there and that another sacrifice was needed.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the law was a shadow of the good things to come, not the full reality. If those sacrifices had cleansed completely, they would no longer have had to be repeated. In this way he prepares the way to show that Christ offered a sufficient sacrifice.

Today, if you live with guilt that keeps returning, remember that in Christ there is complete forgiveness. Bring your sin to him honestly, trust in his finished work, and rest in his grace, without trying to earn forgiveness.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that the blood of animals, such as bulls and male goats, has no real power to take away the sins of people. Here "take away" means to remove or set aside guilt completely. The sacrifices of the law showed how serious sin is, but they could not truly cleanse the conscience at its root.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that the sacrifices offered again every year in the temple pointed to something better. He is preparing them to present Christ, who, through his offered body, dealt with the problem of sin once and for all.

For today: we do not have to carry guilt, trying to make up for our mistakes through efforts, rituals, or good works. We can draw near to God with sincerity, confess our sin, and rest in the forgiveness that Jesus has already won for us.
exp.9:5:
It says that God took no delight in the burnt offerings (offerings completely burned on the altar) or in the sin offerings (sacrifices meant to cover guilt).

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 and presents these words as spoken by Christ when he came into the world. He explains that the blood of animals could not truly take away sins. Those sacrifices, which the law required, pointed to something greater. God prepared a body for Christ, who came to do the Father's will and to offer himself.

For today: let us not trust in rituals or religious efforts to feel clean before God. Let us rest in what Christ has done for us and respond with sincere obedience that springs from a thankful heart.
exp.9:7:
This verse repeats what the writer of Hebrews has just quoted from Psalm 40: God did not want, and took no delight in, the sacrifices and offerings. The word for "offering" means a gift presented to God, and "burnt offering" refers to a sacrifice that was burned up completely. The parenthesis clarifies that these were the things the law of Moses commanded to be offered.

The writer of Hebrews speaks to believers of Jewish background and explains that the ancient sacrifices could not remove sin at its root. He places the words of the psalm in the mouth of Christ, who announces that He would come to do the will of God. In this way he prepares the next step: the old gives way to the new.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through religious effort. Rest in what Christ has already done, and respond with an obedience that comes from gratitude, not from fear.
exp.9:24:
This verse calls us not to stop meeting together as believers, as some have made a habit of doing. Instead, we should encourage one another, and all the more as we see the day drawing near.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians under pressure and tempted to abandon their faith. The verses before this one call them to hold firm and to stir one another up to love and good works. The day is usually understood as the return of Christ and the final judgment, though some also connect it with events close to the author's own time.

For today: find a community of faith and take part in it faithfully. Don't go only to receive, but also to encourage someone with a word, a prayer, or a visit this week.
exp.10:5:
It says that without faith no one can please God. Whoever comes to Him must believe two things: that God exists, and that He rewards those who seek Him.

The author of Hebrews is not identified with certainty; the Bible does not say who wrote it, and several names have been proposed. He writes to believers who were tempted to give up. He has just mentioned Enoch, of whom it is said that he pleased God, and now he explains the reason: he did so by faith. Then he goes on with Noah and Abraham as examples of trust in God.

For today: when you pray, come trusting that God hears you and is good, even if you do not yet see an answer. Continuing to seek Him with perseverance is a simple way of living out faith.
exp.10:7:
What it says: Abraham heard God's call and obeyed. He went out toward a place that God would give him as an inheritance, that is, as a gift that would pass on to his descendants. He did this even though he did not know where he was going.

Context: The author of Hebrews, whose name is not stated in the text, writes to believers who needed to persevere. After saying that without faith it is impossible to please God, and after showing Noah as an example, he presents Abraham. His faith was not just an idea: it was shown in action, and by going out he left what was familiar to follow God's promise.

For today: You may not see the whole road, but God may ask you to take the next step. Trust his character, pray, seek wise counsel, and obey in what he has already shown you, even if you do not yet understand the rest.
exp.10:8:
By faith Abraham lived in the land God had promised him, but as a foreigner would. He had no permanent home; he lived in tents, which were temporary shelters. His son Isaac and his grandson Jacob did the same. The phrase about being "heirs with him of the same promise" means that all three received the same promise from God.

The author of Hebrews is unknown, and tradition has debated who he was. He writes to Jewish believers who were tired and tempted to give up. He gives them examples of faith from people of the past. Abraham believed a promise that he did not see fulfilled in his lifetime, and the verse that follows says he was looking forward to an eternal city, built by God.

For today: we can live with patience when God's promises take a long time. We do not have to cling to what is temporary, because our firmest hope is in God. Trust Him and keep obeying today.
exp.10:9:
This verse says that Abraham was waiting for a city with firm foundations, meaning one that is stable and lasting. Its designer and its builder is God himself. While Abraham lived in tents, he looked toward something more secure than any house in this world.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, encourages tired believers to keep trusting God. To do this, he goes through examples of faith from the Old Testament. Abraham obeyed without knowing his destination and lived as a stranger in the promised land. Many understand that this "city" points to the hope of heaven, although there is debate about how to describe it precisely.

For today: when your plans feel unstable or uncertain, remember that your final security is in God. Live with patience, generosity, and obedience, without clinging too tightly to what is passing.
exp.10:11:
From one man, Abraham, who was already as good as dead (that is, nearly dead, without the strength to have children because of his age), came a descendant as great as the stars of the sky and as the sand on the seashore, too many to count. "On the seashore" is simply the beach.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who needed to persevere. He gives them examples of faith from the Old Testament. Here he recalls that Abraham and Sara trusted that God would fulfill his promise, even though humanly it seemed impossible (Genesis 15:5; 22:17).

For today: when a situation seems closed or without a way out, do not look only at your limitations. God is faithful and can do something great out of something small. Trust in Him, take the next step you know how to take, and wait with patience.
exp.10:12:
This verse says that the heroes of faith mentioned earlier, such as Abraham and Sarah, died trusting God even though they did not see the promises fulfilled. They saw them from a distance, believed them, and welcomed them with joy from afar. They acknowledged that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, travelers just passing through, because their true home was not in this land.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not reveal, writes to believers who were facing pressure and temptation to abandon their faith. He reminds them that others before them waited patiently. Although Sarah and Isaac did see a partial fulfillment, the complete promise still lay ahead.

For today: when a prayer or a dream takes a long time to come true, do not lose heart. Keep trusting God and live as someone who knows that their ultimate hope is in Him.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that those who acknowledge they are foreigners and travelers on the earth make it clear that they are looking for a home of their own, a homeland.

The author of Hebrews is speaking of Abraham, Sara, and other believers of the Old Testament. They died trusting in God's promises, although they did not see them fulfilled. By calling themselves strangers and sojourners on the earth, they showed that their hearts were set on something better than what they had left behind: the heavenly homeland. The author wants to encourage his readers to persevere in faith.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live as those who have placed their hope in God. This does not mean neglecting this life, but not clinging to money, success, or comfort as if they were the final goal. We can live with generosity and patience, remembering that what is best comes from God.
exp.10:15:
They did not long for the country they had left, the author says, but desired something better: a heavenly homeland. For this reason God is not ashamed to be called their God. God had a city ready for them.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who were weary and tempted to turn back. He speaks of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who lived as strangers in Canaan, trusting in promises they did not see fulfilled during their lifetimes. We do not know for certain who wrote the letter, but its message is clear: faith looks forward, not back.

For today: when you feel tempted to return to what God has already brought you out of, remember that He is preparing something better for you. Live with hope and with open hands, not clinging too tightly to what passes away, because your God is not ashamed of you.
exp.10:23:
The explanation says that Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. That is, he turned down the privileges of belonging to the royal family of Egypt. He did this by faith, trusting God more than his own position.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were facing pressure and suffering. He presents them with examples of people from the Old Testament who trusted God. Moses appears alongside Joseph and his own parents. The verses that follow explain his decision: he chose to share the suffering of God's people, looking forward to a future reward.

Today, faith can lead us to give up advantages, comforts, or social approval if they draw us away from God. Ask yourself: is there something I am holding on to that keeps me from being faithful? With God's help, we can choose what is eternal over what is immediate.
exp.10:26:
Moses left Egypt trusting God, and he was not afraid of the anger of the pharaoh. He held on steadily, as though he could see God, even though God is not seen with the eyes. The phrase "him who is invisible" refers to God himself.

The writer of Hebrews recalls the heroes of faith to encourage believers who were under pressure. Some understand this departure to be the exodus with the whole people. Others think it refers to when Moses fled to Midian. The Bible does not make this completely clear, and both views are debated.

When fear of people or of the consequences holds you back, remember that God is present even when you cannot see him. Pray, ask him for courage, and take a step of obedience today, trusting that he sustains you.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel crossed the Red Sea as if it were dry land, and they did it by faith. When the Egyptians tried to do the same, the sea covered them and they were drowned.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, reviews heroes of faith to encourage believers who were facing pressure and suffering. Here he reminds his readers that Israel, just freed from Egypt, trusted God before the sea and the army that was pursuing them. The story is found in Exodus 14.

For today: when you lack a clear path ahead, take the step God shows you, even if you cannot see the whole way. Faith does not wait until everything is clear; it trusts that God knows how to open a way where we see only an obstacle.
exp.10:29:
This verse says that the walls of Jericho fell because the people of Israel trusted God. They walked around the city for seven days, just as God had told them. The word "faith" here means trusting and obeying, even when what is asked does not seem to make sense.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired and tempted to give up. He shows them examples from the past: people who trusted God in difficult moments. He had spoken earlier about the Red Sea, and afterward he mentions Rahab. In this way he reminds them that God keeps what he promises.

For today: when God shows you a step you do not understand, obey it with patience, even if you do not see results right away. Sometimes faith looks like going around day after day, trusting that God will do his work in his own time.
exp.10:30:
This verse says that Rahab, the woman who had been a prostitute, did not perish along with those who did not believe in God. This happened because she had faith and welcomed the spies in peace, that is, she received them kindly and protected them. The unbelievers are those who refused to believe in God and to obey Him. The spies are the men Joshua sent to scout out Jericho.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, gives examples of people who trusted in God and acted accordingly. He has just spoken of the fall of the walls of Jericho. Rahab appears in Joshua 2 and 6: she had heard what God had done for Israel and recognized His power. It is striking that a foreign woman with a marked past is mentioned.

For today: true faith shows itself in concrete actions. No one is outside God's care because of their past. Today you can trust in Him and take a step of obedience, even if it costs you.
exp.10:31:
It says the author has so many examples of faith that there would not be enough time to tell about all of them. He names only a few: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. The phrase about running out of time means he would not have enough time to speak about each one.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were under pressure and were tempted to give up. He has already reviewed the faith of Abraham, Moses, Jericho, and Rahab. Now he speeds up and names several people at once. Many of them were imperfect people, and yet Scripture remembers them for their trust in God.

For today: your faith does not have to be perfect to be real. God worked through weak and fallible people who trusted him. Today you can take a step of obedience, even if you have doubts, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.10:34:
Women received their dead back to life. Others were stretched out on the rack, a word that describes being tortured, probably on an instrument of torment. They did not accept being set free, meaning they refused to be saved by denying their faith, because they were looking forward to a better resurrection.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were under pressure and tempted to give up. He shows them examples of faith from the Old Testament. The cases of women bring to mind the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite woman, in the time of Elijah and Elisha. The cases of torture probably refer to the time of the Maccabees, though this is debated.

Today, this encourages us to stand firm when following God costs something. We can trust that God's hope is worth more than any momentary relief.
exp.10:37:
This verse says the world did not deserve these faithful believers. Although people treated them as if they were disposable, God saw them as very precious. They lived fleeing through deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the earth.

The author of Hebrews (we do not know for certain who he was) writes to believers who were weary and tempted to give up. He shows them a list of people of faith who suffered greatly. The verses that follow say that they waited for God's promise and did not see it fulfilled in full, because God had something better prepared for everyone.

For today: if you face rejection or hardship for following Christ, remember that the world does not define your worth. God sees your faithfulness and invites you to keep trusting, without giving up.
exp.11:0:
This verse says we are surrounded by a great crowd of witnesses, that is, people of faith from the past. For this reason, we should set aside everything that slows us down, above all the sin that tangles us up, and run with endurance, that is, with perseverance, the race that God has set before us.

The author of Hebrews is not known for certain. He writes to Christians who are tired and tempted to give up. Just before, chapter 11 recalls men and women who trusted in God, and these are the witnesses. Many understand that they do not watch us from the stands, but that their example testifies that it is worth trusting in God.

Today you might ask yourself: what habit, burden, or sin is holding me back in my life with God? Ask Him for help to let it go, and keep moving forward with steadiness, looking to Jesus, not to your own strength.
exp.11:12:
It says we should walk on straight paths, with firm and well-directed steps. The explanation notes that one word means straight, and that a person who is "lame" is someone who walks hurt or weak. The idea is that the weak one should not be pushed off the path, but healed.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers worn down by suffering and by God's discipline. We do not know for certain who the author was. He encourages them, and asks that the way they walk help the most fragile members of the community, since the next verse speaks of pursuing peace and holiness.

For today: think of someone in your church or family who is walking weakly in faith. Take care with your example, with consistent choices and kind words, so that your way of living makes their path easier. Walk alongside them with prayer and patience, without judging them.
exp.11:16:
It says that Esau, after selling his birthright, wanted to receive his father's blessing, but he was rejected. The word "rejected" here means turned away or cast off. Although he wept greatly, he found no way to change what he had already done, that is, he could not undo his choice.

The writer of Hebrews is addressing believers who were tired and tempted to abandon their faith. He uses Esau as a warning: Esau despised something sacred for the sake of a passing need. Interpreters debate whether the change of heart he could not find belonged to Esau or to Isaac, but all agree that his tears did not undo the consequences of his decision. It is a serious warning, not a rejection of anyone who seeks God sincerely.

Today we can ask ourselves what valuable parts of our faith we are trading away for comfort or fleeting desires. It is better to return to God today, with a humble heart, and to value what He has given us.
exp.11:17:
This verse says that believers have not come to the mount that could be touched, that is, to a real, physical mountain. It speaks of fire that burned, of a whirlwind or strong wind, of darkness and of tempest. All of that describes how Israel came to Mount Sinai.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were under pressure. He compares Sinai, where the law was given amid fear and distance, with the grace of Christ, which is described in the verses that follow. Earlier he had warned against despising what they had received, as Esau did.

Today, we can draw near to God without paralyzing fear, because Christ opened the way. That is not carelessness: it is humble confidence. Today you can pray with sincerity, remembering that God receives you by grace.
exp.11:18:
This verse recalls what happened at Mount Sinai. A trumpet blast sounded, and a voice spoke. The people were so frightened that they begged that no further word be spoken to them.

The author of Hebrews is writing to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to go back to their old way of life. He shows them what Israel's experience of the law was like: something fearful, marked by fire, darkness, and distance. He does this to set it against what they now have in Christ, which he describes shortly afterward as coming to Mount Zion, not to Sinai.

For today: God is holy and deserves our respect, yet in Christ we can approach Him with confidence. Today you can pray without fear, with reverence and gratitude, remembering that Jesus opened the way.
exp.11:19:
This verse says that the Israelites could not bear the command God gave at Mount Sinai: even if an animal touched the mountain, it had to be stoned or struck through with an arrow.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who were thinking of returning to their former way of life. He recalls what happened in Exodus 19: God revealed himself with fire, smoke, and a trumpet, and he set limits so that the people would understand his holiness. The contrast is that now believers draw near to God through Christ, not in fear before a forbidden mountain.

For today: come near to God with reverence, but also with confidence. He is holy and deserves respect, and at the same time Jesus opened the way for us to pray without fear of being rejected.
exp.11:27:
This verse says that believers receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken or destroyed. So when it speaks of holding on to grace, it means clinging to the favor of God that we have received. With that grace, we serve God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and godly fear, that is, with deep respect and awe before who he is.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were weary and tempted to turn back. He reminds them that at Sinai God's voice shook the earth, and that one day he will shake all that has been created. Only what is firm will remain: the kingdom of God.

For today: when everything around you seems unstable, rest in the fact that you belong to a secure kingdom. Respond with gratitude, serving God with a respectful heart in everyday life: your work, your family, and your decisions.
exp.11:28:
It says God is like a consuming fire. This is an image, not a literal description. Fire burns up what cannot withstand it, and it also purifies. The word "consuming" means that it destroys completely whatever it reaches. In this way, the text shows the holiness of God, who does not tolerate evil.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Christians who are tempted to turn back. He reminds them that everything that can be shaken will be shaken, but the kingdom of God stands firm. For this reason he asks them to serve God with reverence and awe, that is, with deep respect and gratitude. The phrase seems to draw on images from the Old Testament, such as Deuteronomy 4:24.

Today, do not take God lightly. Come to Him with humility and gratitude, and ask Him to burn away in you pride, sin, and everything that does not last. His fire, in Christ, seeks to cleanse you and not to destroy you.
exp.12:0:
It says that love between brothers and sisters in the faith must continue, that is, that it must not go out or grow cold. "Brotherly love" is the affection one has for a brother or sister. "Continue" means to remain steady and constant.

Hebrews is a letter whose author we do not know for certain; scholars hold several opinions. It was written to Jewish believers who were facing pressure and hardship. Here, near the end of the letter, the author gives practical advice for living out the faith. This verse opens that section, and what follows shows how that love is lived out: through hospitality, visiting prisoners, and standing with those who suffer.

Today, think of a brother or sister in your church who is going through a hard time. Call them, visit them, or invite them to a meal this week. In this way love does not stay in words, but continues in simple deeds.
exp.12:1:
This verse asks us not to stop welcoming others warmly, especially those who come from outside. The word "hospitality" here means love for the stranger, that is, opening your home and your table to someone who needs it. "Entertained angels" means they welcomed God's messengers into their homes without realizing it.

The author of Hebrews is not known for certain. He writes to Christians and, at the close of the letter, gives advice for daily life. This phrase explains how brotherly love is lived out. Many think it recalls Abraham and Sarah, and perhaps Lot, who received mysterious visitors, although the text does not name them.

Today you can invite someone new in your church to a meal, a lonely neighbor, or a migrant, without expecting anything in return.
exp.12:2:
It says we should remember those in prison, that is, keep them present in our hearts and in prayer, as if we ourselves were imprisoned with them. The same goes for those who are mistreated and suffering: we should remember them because we too have a body and can suffer. The phrase about the body speaks of our human condition, and perhaps also of the body of Christ.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself; we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to Christians who had endured imprisonment and losses for their faith. Here he gives concrete instructions on how to live out brotherly love: hospitality, solidarity with those who suffer, faithfulness in marriage, and trust in God.

Today we can choose a person who is suffering, such as a prisoner, a sick person, or a brother or sister persecuted for their faith, pray for them by name, and look for a simple way to help them: a visit, a letter, or an offering.
exp.12:8:
It says we should not be carried back and forth by varied and strange teachings. It is good for the heart to be strengthened by God's grace, and not by food rules, that is, rules about what we eat. Those rules never truly helped the people who depended on them.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has just reminded them that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. For that reason they should not change direction because of new teachings. He probably has in mind ritual rules about food and sacrifices, though some think he means other practices.

For today: when a teaching appears that adds requirements for earning God's favor, compare it with Christ and his grace. Keep resting your heart on what Jesus has already done, not on what you manage to accomplish.
exp.12:10:
This verse recalls what happened on the Day of Atonement. The high priest carried the blood of certain animals into the Most Holy Place to ask for forgiveness of sin. But the bodies of those animals were not eaten: they were burned outside the camp of Israel.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to return to their former customs. He uses this image to prepare what follows: Jesus, the final sacrifice, also suffered outside the city gate.

For today: following Christ sometimes means standing outside what others accept or approve. Ask Him for courage to be faithful to Him, even when it costs you rejection, knowing that He has already gone through that and walks with you.
exp.12:11:
It says Jesus died to make his people holy, that is, to set them apart for God and cleanse them, and he did this with his own blood. His suffering took place outside the gate, that is, outside the walls of Jerusalem. To be made holy means to be dedicated and made belonging to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were pressured to return to their old rituals. He compares Jesus to the animals of the Day of Atonement, whose bodies were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16). Jesus was rejected and crucified outside the city, but there he accomplished something greater than those sacrifices.

For today: following Jesus may cost us approval or comfort. If you feel rejected for being faithful to him, remember that he went through this before, and that his blood has already made you his. Be encouraged to be faithful without being ashamed.
exp.12:12:
It says we should go out to Jesus, outside the camp, and bear the disgrace he endured. The word for camp in this verse refers to the camp itself, and the disgrace is the shame and scorn that come with it. Jesus died outside the city gate, just as the bodies of the animals whose blood was taken into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background who were under pressure and facing rejection. He reminds them of the ritual of the Day of Atonement and asks them not to return to the safety of the old system. Some understand "the camp" as the temple-centered Judaism of that time; others understand it as any religious or social system that rejects Christ.

Today, following Jesus can cost us approval or comfort. When you find yourself misunderstood for living with honesty and faith, remember that he was already there, and go with him with confidence.
exp.12:13:
This verse says that in this world we do not have a city that lasts forever. For that reason, believers seek the future city that God is preparing.

The author of Hebrews wrote to believers who were suffering rejection for following Jesus. He says that Jesus suffered outside the gate, that is, outside Jerusalem, and he invites us to go out to him outside the camp, bearing his disgrace.
