The identity of the writer of the book is not known with certainty. Afterward, the text speaks of praising God and helping others.

Today we can live with open hands: not clinging to material things or to the applause of others. With that hope, let us use our time and resources to praise God and do good to those around us.
exp.12:16:
The explanation says that believers should obey their pastors, that is, the leaders of the church, and respect their guidance. The reason is that they watch over the souls of the congregation and will one day have to give account to God. In this way they can do their work with joy and not with grief. Watching means being alert, like a guard. Their watching is done with sorrow and complaint, which is why the verse warns that grief would be of no benefit to you.

The author of Hebrews is unknown; the letter does not give his name. He writes to Christians who needed to persevere. He comes from speaking about praising God and helping others, and moves on to how to live together in community. He asks for prayer for himself, so he also belongs to that circle of leaders and brothers.

For today: pray for your leaders and listen to their teaching with humility, always comparing it with the Bible. Encourage them with a kind word, and support them with your service in the church.
exp.12:20:
It says that God, the God of peace mentioned in the previous verse, is the one who prepares and equips believers to do every good thing and to carry out his will. He himself works in them what pleases him, and he does this through Jesus Christ. For that reason, glory is given to Christ forever.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the letter does not mention (tradition has proposed several and there is no certainty), closes his message with a prayer of blessing. After urging his readers to persevere and to live faithfully, he now places his trust in God, not in human strength.

For today: when you want to do good but feel weak, ask God to equip you and to work in you. Obedience does not depend only on your own effort; God gives you what you need through Jesus.
exp.9:27:
Under the law of Moses, a person who rejected it and was accused by two or three witnesses died without anyone showing them pity. "Rejected" means refusing to accept something or treating it as having no value. "Without pity" means that once the wrongdoing was proven, the punishment was not eased.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon Christ. He reminds them how serious it was to disobey the old law, to show that rejecting Christ, who is greater than Moses, is even more serious. The verses that follow make this comparison. Scholars debate how to understand the "willful sin" in the previous verse, but all of them see here a warning against deliberately turning away from Christ.

Today, do not take God's grace lightly. If you have felt the urge to step away from Christ, return to Him with humility and value what it cost to be forgiven.
exp.11:14:
We are told to look out for one another so that no one falls short of the grace of God, that is, his favor and help, which none of us deserves. It also warns that no root of bitterness should spring up: a resentment that takes hold, grows, and does damage. To be defiled means to be stained or harmed. To cause trouble means that it creates problems for you and for others.

Context: the author of Hebrews, who does not name himself in the letter, writes to believers who are weary and pressed by hardships. He urges them to persevere, to pursue peace, and to pursue holiness. The image of a root of bitterness recalls Deuteronomy 29:18. Right after this, he gives the example of Esau, who traded what was precious for something fleeting.

For today: if you hold a grudge against someone, do not let it grow. Bring it to God, ask his help to forgive, and, if possible, seek reconciliation before that bitterness affects you and others.
exp.6:24:
He is able to save completely and forever those who draw near to God through him. "Save completely" can be understood as saving fully, or to the very end. "Draw near" means to come close. And because Jesus lives forever, he intercedes, that is, he asks and speaks on their behalf before God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares Jesus with the ancient priests, who died and had to be replaced. Jesus, by contrast, lives forever, and his priesthood does not pass to another or come to an end. For that reason his help never stops.

Today you can come near to God with confidence, even when you feel weak or guilty. You do not depend on your own steadiness, but on Jesus, who lives and prays for you. When you pray, do so remembering that he is already interceding on your behalf.
exp.7:4:
The writer says that the priests on earth served in a place that was only a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. This is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: he was told to make everything according to the pattern shown him on the mountain.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a superior High Priest. The worship of the tabernacle was good, but it pointed to something greater, and that greater thing is fulfilled in Christ and in his heavenly ministry.

For today: do not cling to what is only a sign or shadow, such as rituals or customs, and neglect Christ, who is the reality. Let your faith rest in him and not only in outward forms.
exp.10:22:
The explanation says that Moses' parents hid him for the first three months after his birth. They did this because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king's edict. The word "edict" means an official order or decree.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, is recalling people of faith from the Old Testament to encourage his readers to keep trusting God. According to Exodus 1 and 2, the pharaoh had ordered that the Hebrew baby boys be killed. The text credits the action to the parents' faith, not simply to human cleverness. Some think the word for "beautiful" suggests that they saw God's hand in him, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: faith is sometimes seen in simple, brave decisions, such as protecting someone vulnerable even when it is frightening. Trust God and do the right thing within your reach, even when you cannot see the whole future.
exp.11:22:
This verse continues to describe where believers in Christ have come. It speaks of "the joyful assembly and congregation of the firstborn," that is, the family of God's children who have an inheritance and a special place, whose names are "enrolled" in heaven, meaning recorded there. It also mentions God as the Judge of all, and "the spirits of the righteous made perfect," which many understand to be God's faithful people already made complete by Christ.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to Jewish Christians who were tempted to turn back because of their trials. He compares Mount Sinai, full of terror, with Mount Zion, where God receives us by grace. Some interpret "firstborn" as the whole church; others understand it as believers already in heaven.

For today: if your name is enrolled in heaven, do not live in fear or alone. You belong to a great family. Pray and serve with that assurance, trusting that Christ has made you acceptable before God.
exp.6:15:
He says that Jesus was not made priest by a human rule based on family line or descent. In the law of Moses, priests had to come from the tribe of Levi. Jesus was made priest by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed. "Indestructible" means that it cannot be wiped out or brought to an end.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, is a different and greater priest, like Melchizedek. His priesthood does not depend on a family line, but on his resurrection and his life that cannot be destroyed.

Today you can trust that your Savior lives and never stops interceding for you. Your relationship with God does not depend on your record or your merits, but on Christ, who lives forever.
exp.12:18:
The author asks for prayer with even more urgency: "And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon." He wants the readers to pray for him, and his reason is that he hopes to come back to them soon.

The author of Hebrews does not give his name, and we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to a Christian community that he knows and from which, for some reason, he is separated. The text does not explain the reason: it could be a journey, a hardship, or a prison. At the close of the letter, he asks for their prayers with humility and confidence, like someone who needs the support of his brothers and sisters.

Today we can learn that praying for one another is a real act of love and unity. Think of someone in your church, or a pastor, who is far away or going through a trial. Pray for that person by name today, and if you can, let them know you did.
exp.9:19:
He says that Jesus opened for us a new and living way toward God. The word "opened" means that he began it, making a way that had never been available before. That way passes through the curtain, which was the veil of the temple that separated the Most Holy Place, and the text identifies this curtain with his body, given up on the cross.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to give up. He reminds them that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient and that no further offerings for sin are needed. For this reason he encourages them to draw near to God with confidence. There are different views on how exactly to understand the image of the curtain, but the central idea is clear: Christ opened the way of access.

For today: when you feel far from God or unworthy, do not wait to make yourself presentable first. Pray with confidence, because Jesus has already opened the door.
exp.3:8:
There remains a rest prepared for those who belong to God. The word "rest" points to peace, relief, and calm. The idea that it "remains" means the promise is still open and available; it has not run out.

The writer of Hebrews is speaking to believers who were tempted to give up. He reminds them that Israel did not enter that rest because of their disobedience, and that even Joshua, when he led them into the promised land, did not fully fulfill that promise. That is why David spoke of another "today." Christians understand this rest as resting in God and trusting in his work, with a fullness that will be completed in the future. There are different ways of explaining it.

Today you can stop living to earn God's favor through your own effort. Pause, trust in him, and hand him your burdens with faith and obedience.
exp.4:10:
It says that the author has much to explain about Christ as priest according to the order of Melchizedek, but that it is hard to put into words. The reason is not that the subject is bad, but that the readers are "dull of hearing," that is, slow or lazy to understand and listen.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who had been in the faith for a long time, but had become stuck. He has just mentioned Melchizedek and wants to go deeper, but he pauses to correct them kindly. He reminds them that they should already be teaching others, and not need to have the basics repeated to them.

For today: ask yourself whether you are growing in your faith or just repeating what you have always done. Set aside time regularly to read the Bible carefully and to ask God for a heart willing to learn deeper things.
exp.2:8:
The verse says that the ancestors of Israel tested God in the desert. Here, "tested" means putting God's patience to the test by doubting Him. Even so, for forty years they saw the works of God: the manna, the water from the rock, His daily care. "Your fathers" are the Israelites who came out of Egypt.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and says that the Holy Spirit is the one speaking. He writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to abandon their faith in Christ. He reminds them that seeing God's works is not enough if the heart becomes hard. God is the one speaking in the quotation, and that is why the text goes on to speak of His anger and His oath.

Today: do not get so used to God's blessings that you begin to doubt Him. When a difficulty comes, remember what He has already done for you and trust Him, with a heart ready to obey Him today.
exp.9:26:
It says that for someone who deliberately rejects the truth of Christ, only a terrible judgment remains to be awaited. The word "fearful" here means dreadful, and "expectation" means an anticipation of what is coming, not something good. The "raging fire" is an image of God's anger that will consume His "adversaries," that is, those who oppose Him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians tempted to abandon their faith under pressure. He warns them that turning back after knowing Christ is rejecting the only sacrifice that forgives. Christians have debated whether he is speaking of true believers or of those who only seemed to be.

For today: do not walk away from the community or from Christ when everything gets hard. Seek the support of other believers, and if you have failed, return to Jesus with humility, for in Him forgiveness remains.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that Jesus, after offering his sacrifice, is seated at the right hand of God and waits. The phrase "since that time" refers to the period that continues until the end. A footstool was a small stool where the feet rested; placing enemies there means their total defeat.

The author of Hebrews compares the priests, who offered sacrifices again and again, with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for all time. That is why he has already sat down: his work is finished. Here the author draws on Psalm 110:1. His purpose is to encourage believers who were doubting, showing that Christ is superior and that his final victory is certain.

For today: you can rest in the fact that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts, but on what Christ has already done. And although you see evil in the world, you can wait with patience and confidence, because God will fulfill his promise in his time.
exp.0:7:
Here God the Father speaks to his Son and says, "Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever." The phrase "forever and ever" means for all eternity. The "scepter" is a king's staff of rule, and in this verse it is said to be a scepter of justice. His kingdom is governed with perfect justice.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 45 to show that Jesus is superior to the angels. The angels are servants and messengers, but the Son is addressed as God and is given an eternal kingdom. In this way the writer encourages Jewish believers to trust in Christ and not to abandon him.

For today: when everything seems unjust or unstable, remember that Jesus reigns, and his rule is just and does not end. Entrust your decisions and your worries to him, and seek to live with the same justice that he loves.
exp.6:2:
The explanation says that Melchizedek appears in Scripture with no mention of father or mother or family line, and with no record of his beginning or his end. The words "genealogy" and "like" in the passage refer to a family record and to resemblance. In the account, Melchizedek therefore serves as a picture of the Son of God, whose priesthood remains for all time.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old ways. He uses the silence of Genesis 14 about Melchizedek to show that Christ's priesthood is greater than that of Levi. Some understand that Melchizedek was a real man described with this purpose in view; others understand him to be a special appearance of Christ. The Bible does not fully settle the matter.

Today you can rest in the fact that Jesus is your permanent priest. His care for you does not depend on taking turns and does not come to an end, so you can approach God with confidence at any time.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that the new covenant would not be like the one God made with Israel when he brought them out of Egypt. God remembers that moment with tenderness: he took them by the hand. But the people did not abide by his covenant; they were not faithful to it. The phrase "I disregarded them" means that God stopped looking after them as a people under that covenant; some understand it as God turning away from them with sorrow.

The author of Hebrews quotes the prophet Jeremiah (31:31-34). He writes to believers of Jewish background to show them that Jesus brings a better covenant, because the old one depended on human faithfulness, and that faithfulness failed.

For today: let us not trust in our own steadfastness, but in the work of Christ. God holds us by the hand, and through his grace he changes our hearts from within.
exp.2:11:
This verse is a warning to believers. "See to it" means "be careful, pay attention." A "wicked heart of unbelief" is a heart that stops trusting God, and "turns away" describes drifting away little by little. "The living God" reminds us that God is real and active, not a lifeless idol.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. He quotes Psalm 95, which speaks of Israel in the wilderness. That generation saw the works of God, yet they doubted and rebelled, and for that reason they did not enter the rest of the promised land. The author uses that example as a warning.

Today, unbelief almost never arrives all at once; it grows through small doubts and neglect. Seek the encouragement of other believers, as the next verse says, and each day bring your doubts to God in prayer, trusting in his Word.
exp.12:14:
Through Jesus, believers are to offer God a sacrifice of praise at all times. That sacrifice is "the fruit of lips that confess His name," meaning words that openly declare and honor God. The word "to" in the verse simply points to the one receiving the offering, and "confess" here means openly declaring, giving thanks, and proclaiming.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were suffering rejection and pressure. He reminds them that Jesus suffered outside the gate and that they do not have a permanent city here. Since they no longer offer the sacrifices of the temple, he tells them that their offering now is praise, together with doing good.

Today, even in difficult days, we can speak aloud a sincere gratitude to God: when we wake up, at work, or in the family. Praising does not depend on how we feel, but on who God is.
exp.11:11:
This verse encourages weary believers to regain their strength. The phrase "strengthen" means to make something firm again, and "limp" describes hands that have gone slack and weak, no longer able to grip well. "Weak" describes knees that are feeble and loose, no longer holding a person up well. It is the picture of someone exhausted in a race.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who were going through hardships. He has just explained that God's discipline, though painful, is a sign that he treats us as his children and produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness. For this reason, the verse begins with "Therefore": since God corrects us for our good, we should not give up. The verses that follow call for walking straight and helping those who are lame.

For today: if you are tired from a trial, do not stay fallen. Take one small step today, pray, go to church, or seek out a brother or sister who can encourage you, and do the same for someone who is weak.
exp.1:0:
It says that we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. The phrase "must" means that this is required. Paying closer attention is the idea of giving careful focus. The image of drifting away is of something that slides off without our noticing, like a boat carried off by the current.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself; we do not know with certainty who he is. He writes to Christians of Jewish background, and he has just shown that Jesus is superior to the angels. That is why he says "therefore": since the Son is so great, his message deserves our full attention. The verses that follow warn that we must not neglect a salvation so great.

For today: we usually do not drift away all at once, but slowly, through carelessness. Set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible and pray, and look for a community of believers who can help you stay firm.
exp.6:13:
It says that everyone knows that Jesus, our Lord, came from the tribe of Judah. And Moses said nothing about priests coming from that tribe. "Clear" means plain and easy to see. "Concerning" means "about." According to the law, priests came from the tribe of Levi, not from Judah.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is a different kind of priest, in the style of Melchizedek, and not in the style of Levi. If the priesthood changes, the law that supported it changes too. Jesus did not fit the old system, and that is why God was doing something new.

For today: you do not need a go-between or a special ritual to draw near to God. Jesus is your priest, and through Him you can pray with confidence, today, just as you are.
exp.9:20:
This verse says that believers have a "great priest" over the "house of God." A priest was the one who presented the people before God. Here Jesus is spoken of as that great priest. The "house of God" refers to his people, the family of those who believe in him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whom we cannot identify with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. Earlier he spoke of Jesus' single sacrifice. Now he summarizes: thanks to him we can draw near to God with boldness, and this prepares the invitation that follows: let us draw near with a sincere heart in faith.

For today: when you feel unworthy or far from God, remember that Jesus is already interceding for you. Pray with confidence, without fear, because you do not go alone; you have someone who represents you and receives you.
exp.11:24:
It tells us to be careful not to refuse God when he speaks to us. "Refuse" means to reject or turn away from, and "escape" means to get away from the consequences. If the people of old did not get away when they refused the one who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject the one who warns us from heaven?

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were weary and tempted to turn back. He compares Moses and Sinai, where God spoke on earth, with Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant. Since Jesus' blood speaks better than the blood of Abel, his message deserves even more attention.

Today we can listen to God with humility every day, by reading his Word and obeying what he shows us, instead of putting it off or making excuses.
exp.12:23:
Hebrews 13:24 asks the readers to greet all their leaders, meaning those who guide and care for them, and also all the saints, meaning all the believers. Then it passes along greetings from those from Italy. The word "saints" does not describe people who are perfect, but people who belong to God. The greeting is addressed to "all," so the reader is asked to greet everyone in both groups.

The author of Hebrews closes his letter with farewells. We do not know for certain who wrote it, and this has been much debated. The words "those from Italy" may mean that he is writing from Italy, or that he is sending greetings from people from Italy who are with him, and not everyone agrees on which is meant. Either way, the closing shows warmth toward his readers, whom he had earlier urged to persevere.

Today we can value those who care for us spiritually. This week, greet or write a few words of thanks to your pastor or some leader, and also to a brother who may feel lonely. A simple greeting strengthens unity.
exp.3:10:
He calls us to make every effort to enter God's rest, and to take that seriously. He also warns that no one should fall by following the same pattern of disobedience, that is, that no one should repeat the mistake of not trusting and not obeying God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who could grow weary or turn back. He reminds them of the people of Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the rest promised to them because of their unbelief. He then adds that the Word of God reveals what is in the heart.

Today, trusting God requires a daily decision. When you feel tired or tempted to rely only on yourself, pause, pray, and obey what God has already shown you in his Word.
exp.11:25:
At that time God's voice shook the earth, as it did at Mount Sinai. But now he has made a greater promise: "Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well." The words "once more" point to a final shaking, one that reaches beyond the earth.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who faced pressure and temptation to abandon their faith. He quotes the prophet Haggai (2:6) and recalls Sinai to warn them: if it was serious to refuse God when he spoke on the earth, it is even more serious to refuse him when he speaks from heaven through Jesus.

For today: when everything around you seems unstable, rely on what does not move, the kingdom of God. Listen carefully to his voice and respond to him with confidence and reverence.
exp.7:1:
Here Hebrews says that Jesus, our high priest, serves in the sanctuary in heaven, which the text calls the true tabernacle. This sanctuary was not set up by any human being but by the Lord himself. "High priest" means chief priest, a "minister" is someone who serves, and "set up" means that the Lord established it.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to temple practices. He summarizes his argument for them: Jesus is seated beside God and serves in the heavenly sanctuary, which is superior to the earthly tabernacle. Scholars debate whether this sanctuary is a literal place or an image of God's presence, but the text emphasizes that its origin is divine.

Today, you can approach God with confidence, because Jesus intercedes for you in a place that no one can harm. You do not need to earn access through your own efforts.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that when a will is in place, it is necessary to establish the death of the one who made it. The person who leaves an inheritance is the one who made the will, and that person's death must be established for the will to take effect.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that Christ is the mediator of the new covenant. The Greek word used here can be translated as "will" or as "covenant," and scholars debate how it applies in this passage. In either case, the central idea is that Jesus' death makes possible the promised eternal inheritance.

Today we can receive salvation as a gift, not as a wage we earn. This week, thank God for what Christ has done, and live with the confidence of someone who has already been included in the inheritance.
exp.0:2:
The Son is the radiance of God's glory, showing the Father's greatness the way a light shines out from its source, and he is the exact representation of God's nature. He also holds up everything that exists by his powerful word. After he had provided purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, the place of honor and authority beside God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He shows them that God no longer spoke only through the prophets, but through his Son, who is greater than the prophets and the angels.

For today: if Jesus holds up all things and has already provided purification for your sin, you can rest in him. When you feel guilty or afraid, trust in his finished work and in his constant care.
exp.4:5:
This verse quotes another passage of Scripture (Psalm 110:4) to show that God himself appointed Christ as priest. "Forever" means without end. "In the order of Melchizedek" means that his priesthood is like that of Melchizedek, a king and priest from the time of Abraham, and not like that of Aaron.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) is writing to believers of Jewish background. He explains that Jesus did not give himself the office of high priest, but that God called him to it. First he cites Psalm 2:7, and then Psalm 110:4, to confirm that calling.

For today: you can trust that Jesus serves as priest on your behalf forever. His help does not end and does not depend on you, so draw near to God in prayer with confidence, without fear.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that Jesus Christ does not change: he is the same in the past, in the present, and in the future. "Forever" means "for all time." His character, his love, and his power remain firm.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were facing pressures. He reminds them of their former leaders, who taught them the faith and lived it. Those leaders were no longer there, but Christ remains. Because of this, the author then warns them against strange teachings that could lead them astray.

When everything around you changes, such as your work, your health, or the people in your life, you can lean on someone who does not change. Today, in prayer, hand over one worry and remember how Christ has been faithful before. His past faithfulness is a reason to trust him now.
exp.12:24:
It says that grace, that is, God's undeserved favor and help, be with all of you. "Grace be with all of you" is a short closing blessing. The word "Amen" is not included in this version, so there is no need to explain it.

The author of Hebrews does not name himself, and we do not know for certain who he was. He closes the letter with a simple greeting and a wish for blessing on the whole community. The closing note about Italy and Timothy found in some other ancient copies is not part of this verse, and it is a later tradition that cannot be verified. What is clear is that he writes with pastoral care to believers who needed to persevere.

For today: when you say goodbye to someone, truly bless them. You can offer a brief prayer or a word of encouragement, remembering that we live by God's grace and not by our own strength.
exp.7:7:
This verse says that God, while pointing out the failure of his people, announced that days would come when he would make a new covenant with Israel and Judah. The phrase "found fault with them" means that God pointed out their error and their failure to keep the covenant.

The author of Hebrews quotes the prophet Jeremiah (31:31-34). He writes to believers of Jewish background and wants to show them that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant than the one given through Moses. The problem did not lie in God's law, but in the fact that the people did not remain faithful. That is why God promised something new, one that reaches the heart.

For today: do not rely on your own strength to be faithful to God. He offers you a new relationship through Christ and can transform you from the inside. Ask him each day that his Word take root in your heart.
exp.9:21:
The explanation says that we can approach God with a sincere heart, trusting fully in Him. It explains that the verse's wording means "let us come near." It also says that "full assurance" means firm confidence. It speaks of having the heart cleansed from a guilty conscience and the body washed with clean water. Many understand this as an image of baptism; others see it as a picture of spiritual purification in general.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to lose heart or turn back. He reminds them that Jesus, our great priest, opened a new way to God. Before, only the priest entered the most holy place. Now all of us can draw near through Christ.

For today: when you feel guilty or unworthy, do not turn away from God. Pray honestly, confess what weighs on your conscience, and trust that Jesus has already opened the door. Come near today, just as you are.
exp.1:13:
It says that the "children," that is, the believers, have flesh and blood, meaning they are human beings. For this reason Jesus also shared in their humanity, fully and truly. He did this so that by his death he might destroy the devil, who holds the power of death. The word "destroy" can be understood as to take away its strength or to make it powerless.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know with certainty, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has just quoted Old Testament passages where Christ calls his people his "brothers." Now he explains why Jesus had to share our humanity: to rescue us from within our very condition.

For today: if you fear death, suffering, or the future, remember that Jesus went through these things and overcame them. He understands you and is with you. You can pray with confidence and live with hope.
exp.2:13:
We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first. That is, we share in his life and his blessings on the condition that we remain steady to the end in the trust we had when we began. Here "hold firmly" means to keep a firm grip on something and not let go, and "assurance" means confidence and faith in God.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to Jewish Christians who were tempted to give up. He reminds them of the people of Israel, who left Egypt but hardened their hearts in the wilderness through unbelief. He warns that true faith shows itself by persevering. Some Christians read this as a warning that salvation can be lost; others read it as proof that genuine faith endures. Both agree on the need to persevere.

Today you can encourage someone in your church or family with a word of comfort, and you can also let yourself be encouraged. In this way faith stays alive in difficult days.
exp.1:10:
For both the One who makes us holy and those who are made holy come from one and the same family. For this reason Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers. Jesus sets us apart and cleanses us for God, and we are the ones being made holy, and both belong to God the Father.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who needed encouragement. He has just explained that Jesus became human and suffered in order to bring many children to glory. For this reason Jesus can identify with us. The verses that follow quote the Psalms and Isaiah to show that family bond.

For today: even when you sometimes feel unworthy or full of faults, Christ is not ashamed of you. Come to him with confidence, as to a brother who understands you, and treat other believers with affection too, because they are your family.
exp.9:22:
This verse invites us to hold firmly to the hope we declare, without giving in to doubt or drifting from it. "Hold resolutely" means to keep a steady grip on something, and the hope in view is the hope we openly confess. The reason is simple: God is faithful, and he keeps what he has promised.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians who were weary and tempted to give up. He has just explained that Jesus is the great priest who opens the way to God for us. For that reason he now encourages them to draw near with confidence, not to let go of their hope, and to stay united.

For today: when you doubt or feel weary, remember a specific promise of God and repeat it in prayer. Also, look for other believers who can encourage you, because faith is better sustained in company.
exp.11:2:
Consider Jesus closely, the one who endured such hostility from sinners. The phrase "consider him" simply means to think carefully about him or look closely at him. "Hostility" refers to open hatred and rejection. Growing weary means becoming so exhausted that you give up. The purpose is that we do not wear ourselves out or lose heart.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired from pressure and hardship. He has just compared the life of faith to a race and pointed to Jesus, who suffered the cross and now sits in honor with God. Next he reminds them that they have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood for their faith.

When you feel worn out by opposition or trials, spend a few minutes reading about how Jesus faced rejection. Ask him for strength to keep going without giving up.
exp.10:4:
By faith Enoch was taken up by God so that he did not see death. People could not find him, because God had taken him away. Before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers to encourage them to keep going in their faith. He presents examples of faith from the Old Testament: Abel, then Enoch, then Noah. Genesis 5:24 tells that Enoch walked with God. The following verse explains that without faith it is impossible to please God.

For today: pleasing God is not a matter of doing extraordinary things, but of walking with Him each day, trusting that He exists and rewards those who seek Him. Today you can set aside a few minutes to speak with Him and entrust Him with your day.
exp.9:35:
It says we need perseverance, meaning steady endurance, to keep doing what God wants and so receive what He has promised. The phrase "you need" means that they need it. "Will receive" is what the verse says in place of the word for obtaining. Perseverance is not standing still, but staying faithful in obeying God while the promise arrives.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers who had already suffered: some were imprisoned, and others lost their possessions. Now they were at risk of growing tired and giving up. So he reminds them of their earlier faith, speaks to them of a better inheritance in heaven, and encourages them not to let go of their confidence, for the coming of the Lord will not be delayed.

For today: when obeying God costs you something or the answer takes a long time, do not give up. Choose one concrete step of faithfulness today, such as praying, forgiving, or serving, and trust that God fulfills what He promises.
exp.6:14:
This verse says that what the author has been explaining becomes even more clear: God has appointed another priest who is like Melchizedek. The word "clear" means plain and easy to see. The idea of a priest appearing means that he is raised up or appointed by God. It refers to Jesus.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers from a Jewish background. He shows them that Jesus is a priest, even though he came from the tribe of Judah and not from Levi, which was the priestly tribe. For that reason a different pattern was needed: Melchizedek, a priest who came before the law of Moses.

For today: you do not need intermediaries or personal merits to draw near to God. Jesus is your priest forever. Today you can pray with confidence, knowing that he represents you before the Father.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that God promises to remember our sins and our lawless acts no more. The word "lawless acts" refers to deeds that break God's law or ignore it. The word "adds" continues the quotation from Jeremiah 31 that comes from the previous verse. "Will remember no more" does not mean that God forgets, but that He no longer holds them against us.

The author of Hebrews explains that the Holy Spirit spoke in the Scripture about the new covenant. He writes to believers of Jewish background, and he wants to show that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient. That is why, in the following verse, he says that no other offering for sin is needed any longer.

For today: if you have trusted in Christ, do not carry guilt for sins that have already been forgiven. When you remember a past mistake, bring it to God with gratitude, learn from it, and live in freedom and confidence.
exp.8:14:
He says that Jesus is the mediator of a new covenant. His death took place to redeem people from the transgressions committed under the first covenant. So those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.

The book of Hebrews was written to believers with a Jewish background; no one knows for certain who its author was. It had been comparing the sacrifices in the temple with the sacrifice of Christ. The animals cleansed the outward person, but Christ cleanses the conscience. The Greek word can mean "covenant" or "testament," and the following verses play on both meanings.

If you feel guilty for past failures, remember that Christ has already paid with his death. You can come before God with confidence, not to earn his favor, but to serve him with gratitude.
exp.3:2:
Now we who have believed enter that rest. This verse says that God's rest is open to those who trust Him, while others will not enter it. God's words of judgment, "They shall never enter My rest," are a solemn oath, and the verse contrasts those who believe with those who do not. And this is so even though God's works have been finished since the foundation of the world.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who could become discouraged. He quotes Psalm 95, where God spoke about the people of Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the promised land because of their lack of faith. The author warns that the promise still stands and that hearing it is not enough: it must be believed.

Today, faith is not only hearing the Word, but trusting in it. If you are tired of struggling to earn God's favor, rest in what Christ has done and keep trusting in Him each day.
exp.6:6:
Hebrews 7:7 says that, beyond any doubt, the one who blesses is greater than the one who is blessed. "Doubt" here means dispute or questioning. The lesser is the one in the lower place, and the greater is the one who holds the higher position.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show that Melchizedek is greater than Abraham, because Melchizedek blessed him and received tithes from him. So the priesthood of Melchizedek, which points to Christ, is greater than the Levitical priesthood.

Today we can remember that Jesus is greater than every tradition, ritual, or religious leader. Before trusting in anything to feel accepted by God, return to Christ, our great high priest, and rest in his complete work.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain, and that he did so by faith. Because of that faith, he was commended as righteous, and God gave approval to his gifts. Although Abel died, his faith still speaks to us today.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers who needed to keep trusting God. In chapter 11 he presents people from the Old Testament who lived by faith. Abel is the first on the list. The text stresses that his sacrifice was better because of his faith, not only because of what he offered. Genesis 4 tells the story, though it does not explain in detail why God accepted one offering and not the other.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our service to God springs from trust in Him or only from habit. God looks at the heart. We can offer Him our time, work, and worship with sincerity and faith.
exp.0:3:
He says that Jesus, the Son of God, is far superior to the angels. The word "excellent" means better, greater. The name he has inherited is the name "Son," which God never gave to any angel, and it is this name that sets him above them.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known with certainty, writes to Christians of Jewish background. They held the angels in great respect, since they believed God gave the law through them. The author wants to show that Christ is greater than all that came before, and for that reason it is worth following him with firmness, even in the midst of difficulties.

When life becomes hard or you feel tempted to look for support in other things, remember who Jesus is: the Son, the one who upholds all things and cleansed your sins. Trust in him above all.
exp.5:0:
Leaving behind the basic teachings about Christ, the believer is urged to move on toward maturity (the word here means growing, becoming complete). The foundation does not need to be laid again: repenting of dead works (actions that do not give life before God) and believing in God.

The author of Hebrews is unknown; the letter is addressed to believers with a Jewish background who were tempted to turn back. He rebuked them for still acting like children in the faith (5:12-14). That is why he calls them to mature. Some think this list of basic teachings reflects practices known in Judaism, but this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: foundations are important, but a house does not stay only at the foundation. Make time a steady habit of reading the Bible, praying, and serving, so that your faith keeps growing and does not stall.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that Sarah, although she was barren and past the proper age, was enabled to conceive a child. The phrase "enabled to conceive" points to a power she received, not one she produced herself. The word "seed" means descendants, so the verse is speaking of the children who would come from her. She was able to do this because she considered God faithful to what he had promised.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who needed to persevere. He reviews examples of faith from the Old Testament. Earlier he spoke of Abraham, who lived as a foreigner while waiting for God's promise. Here he highlights Sarah, whose trust in a faithful God opened the way to a great number of descendants.

For today: when a situation seems impossible or far too late, remember that your trust rests on the faithfulness of God and not on your own strength. Today you can bring to him in prayer what you are hoping for, and choose to trust that he keeps what he promises.
exp.11:26:
This verse says that the words "Once more" announce a change: God will remove what can be shaken, that is, created things, so that what is unshakable will remain. "Shaken" means moved or made to tremble, and what can be shaken is anything that can be moved or disturbed.

The writer of Hebrews quotes the prophet Haggai (2:6) and warns believers not to refuse God when he speaks. When God spoke at Sinai, the earth shook. Now he speaks from heaven, and the warning is even more serious. Many understand that the kingdom of God is the only thing that cannot be shaken, although interpreters debate exactly how this will be fulfilled.

For today: do not place your security in things that can fall, such as money, work or reputation. Rest on Christ and on his kingdom, and respond to his voice with gratitude and reverence.
exp.12:6:
This verse asks us to remember the leaders who spoke the word of God to us. The phrase "your leaders" points to those who guide and lead the community. It also invites us to imitate their faith, thinking carefully about the outcome of how they lived.

The letter to the Hebrews does not say with certainty who wrote it. It is addressed to believers of Jewish background who faced pressure and temptations to turn back. Earlier, the author encouraged them to live without greed and to trust that God never abandons them. Later, he reminds them that Jesus Christ does not change, and so they should not be carried away by strange teachings.

Today we can thank those who taught us the faith, perhaps a pastor, a grandmother, or a teacher. Think of one person whose life was faithful to God, and imitate one concrete virtue of theirs this week.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that Levi, the ancestor of the Jewish priests, paid the tenth to Melchizedek through Abraham when Abraham paid it. The phrase "so to speak" signals that the author is putting it in a figurative way. Levi had not yet been born, but he was, in a sense, within his great-grandfather Abraham.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named and whose identity is debated, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, is greater than the Levitical priesthood. If the very priests descended from Levi honored Melchizedek through Abraham, then Melchizedek's priesthood is greater.

For today: do not place your trust in inherited traditions or achievements. Jesus is our perfect high priest, and through Him we can draw near to God with full confidence.
exp.0:10:
It says that heaven and earth, although they seem firm, will not last forever. They will wear out like old clothing. By contrast, the Lord "remains the same," that is, he does not change or come to an end. The phrase "They will perish" means that they will cease to exist as we know them, and "they will all wear out" means that they will decay over time.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 102:25-27 to show that the Son is superior to the angels. Here the text speaks of the Son as Lord and Creator, since it calls him the one who laid the foundation of the earth. The angels are servants, but the Son is eternal. Some explain that creation will be renewed rather than simply destroyed; the text does not give further details.

Today we can let go of anxiety about things that wear out: money, health, plans. All of that is valuable, but it is not the most secure thing. Place your hope in Christ, who remains the same.
exp.12:22:
He says that Timothy, the fellow worker, "has been released," meaning that he is no longer under restraint or imprisonment. He adds that if Timothy arrives soon, he will come with him to visit you.

The author of Hebrews does not name himself, and we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to Christians of Jewish background who faced pressure and weariness in their faith. It is not known when or where Timothy was imprisoned; the text only says that he has now been released. This closing note shows personal affection after a very deep letter.

For today: faith is lived out in real relationships. Share good news about your brothers and sisters, pray for those who suffer, and stay in touch with them. A phone call or a visit can encourage someone more than you might imagine.
exp.3:13:
It says that we have a great high priest, Jesus, the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens and now stands in the presence of God. "High priest" here means one who brings the people together with God. "What we profess" means what we declare we believe. For that reason, the text encourages us to hold firmly to that faith.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up. He has just spoken of the Word of God that sees everything. Now he comforts them: Jesus is not a distant judge, and in the verses that follow it is said that he understands our weaknesses.

For today: when you feel weak or want to abandon your faith, do not rely only on your own strength. Pray with confidence to Jesus, who understands you, and stay firm one day at a time.
exp.1:5:
Hebrews 2:6 says that someone, in a certain place in Scripture, has spoken these words: what is a human being that God remembers him, and what is the son of man that God cares for him? "But" marks a contrast with what came just before, and "care for" here means to look after and attend to someone.

The writer of Hebrews does not name the speaker, but he quotes Psalm 8, written by David. He wants to show that the world to come will not be placed under the angels, but under human beings, and finally under Jesus, who became a man. Many understand that the phrase "son of man" points to Christ, although it also speaks of humanity in general.

For today: even when you sometimes feel small or overlooked, God remembers you and cares for you. Rest in that, and live with gratitude and dignity.
exp.5:14:
The explanation says that Abraham waited patiently and so received what God had promised him. The phrase "waiting patiently" means that he kept going through the years of delay, neither giving up nor losing hope while he waited. The phrase "obtained the promise" means that he received the fulfillment of what God had told him.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who were tired and tempted to abandon their faith. He gives them the example of Abraham, to whom God promised blessing and many descendants, and confirmed it with an oath. Abraham saw the beginning of the fulfillment, especially with the birth of Isaac, though the full promise reaches beyond his lifetime. Some scholars emphasize this last point; the text itself does not detail it here.

When God has given you a promise and the answer is slow in coming, do not let it go. Keep trusting, praying, and obeying, because patience rests on the fact that God is faithful.
exp.5:3:
This verse begins a sentence that continues in the verses that follow. It says that those who have once been enlightened (who came to understand the truth of the gospel), who have tasted the heavenly gift, and who have shared in the Holy Spirit, and then fall away, cannot be brought back again to repentance. To "fall away" means that they turn away from the faith.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians tempted to abandon Christ. He has just spoken of moving on toward maturity. Christians have interpreted this passage in several ways: some see a real loss of salvation; others see a warning about a false faith or a total and final rejection of Christ.

Today, this text invites us to take our faith seriously. Let us not let it grow cold or abandon it under pressure. Let us cultivate prayer, the Word, and fellowship with other believers every day.
exp.10:35:
This verse speaks of believers who endured mocking and flogging. Mocking is public ridicule and scorn, meant to shame and wear down the person. Flogging is punishment by beating. Some were also held in chains and locked up in prison, deprived of their freedom because of their faith.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whose identity has been much debated, writes to Christians of Jewish background who faced pressure and temptation to abandon Christ. In chapter 11 he reviews the heroes of faith. Earlier he showed those who prevailed with visible victories; now he shows those who also trusted God but suffered. In this way he reminds them that faith does not always bring immediate relief.

Today we can remember that suffering does not mean God has abandoned us or that our faith is weak. If you are mocked or mistreated for following Christ, stand firm, and pray for those who go through persecution.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that if a person has never received discipline from God, something is wrong, because God disciplines all of his children. Here "discipline" means fatherly instruction and correction, not simple punishment meant to make someone suffer. "Illegitimate children" refers to children who are not recognized as true members of the family.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were going through trials and felt discouraged. He reminds them that discipline is not a sign of abandonment, but that God treats them as beloved sons, just as a good father corrects his children.

Today, when God corrects you or you face a difficulty, do not immediately think that he has rejected you. Ask him what he wants to teach you, and receive that correction with humility, trusting that it comes from a Father who loves you.
exp.10:33:
By faith, the heroes of God's people experienced great deliverances. They quenched the raging fire, meaning they put out flames that were extremely strong. They escaped the edge of the sword, that is, they got away from the sword. They gained strength from weakness, and they became mighty in battle, which means they grew strong and brave. They also put foreign armies to flight, making enemy armies run away.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were tired and tempted to give up. He shows them examples from the Old Testament, such as Daniel and his friends, David, and others. He wants to encourage them to keep trusting God. Then he says that others suffered without being delivered, and they also remained faithful.

For today: trust God both when he delivers you and when he asks you to endure. His faithfulness does not depend on the outcome you hope for, and he cares for you in both cases.
exp.4:1:
The explanation says that the high priest is able to deal gently and patiently with those who are ignorant and those who have gone astray, because he himself is subject to weakness. The word translated here as "high priest" is the one the verse itself uses in its context, and the phrase "deal gently" describes treating others with patience, without harshness.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, explains how the priesthood of Israel worked. The priest was a man chosen from among the people, which is why he knew human weakness from the inside. The author is preparing the way to show that Jesus is an even better high priest, who also understands us.

When someone fails or does not understand something, remember your own weaknesses and treat them with patience, not with pride. And if you have failed, draw near to God with confidence: He understands and is merciful.
exp.8:26:
It says that every human being is appointed to die only once, and that after death comes judgment. The word "appointed" means that God has arranged it this way. "Man" here means all people.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He compares the single death of people with the single sacrifice of Christ. The priests offered blood every year, but Jesus offered himself once. In this way, the verse prepares the message that Christ takes away sin and will come again to save those who are waiting for him.

For today: since life is brief and does not repeat, live it with humility and gratitude. Instead of fearing judgment, trust in Christ, who has already borne your sins, and seek today to be reconciled with God and with others.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that Abraham, because he trusted God, was willing to offer Isaac when God tested him. The reader's wording "was tested" matches the phrase, and "only son" is the plain way to say it; Isaac was the child of the promise, although Abraham also had Ishmael. Even so, Abraham acted as one who had already received God's promises.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, encourages believers to remain steadfast. Earlier he spoke of the patriarchs who looked for a heavenly city. Now he shows that Abraham's faith was tested in the hardest way: God had promised him descendants through Isaac, and yet God asked him to offer that son on the altar. The verses that follow explain that Abraham believed God could raise the dead.

For today: trusting God does not always mean understanding his ways. When something we love seems to be at risk, we can entrust it to him in prayer, remembering that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that the blood of Christ has a power far greater than the blood of animals. Christ offered himself to God "unblemished," that is, without sin. "Through the eternal Spirit" can be understood as the Holy Spirit or as the divine nature of Christ; there are different opinions. His sacrifice purifies our consciences from "works of death," which are actions that do not lead to life with God, so that we may now serve the living God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish origin. He explains that the sacrifices in the temple only purified the outward, but Christ offers an inner and lasting cleansing.

For today: if you carry guilt from your past, bring it to God with confidence. Christ has already paid for you, so you can let go of shame and serve God with a clear conscience.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that the Holy Spirit speaks through the Scriptures. The words "if you hear his voice" mean "if you listen" or "if you pay attention." The word "today" stresses that God's voice is heard now, not only in the past.

The author of Hebrews has just said that Christ is greater than Moses and that we are his house if we hold firmly to our confidence. Now he quotes Psalm 95 and attributes it to the Holy Spirit. He does this as a warning: the people of Israel in the wilderness heard God, but they hardened their hearts. The sentence continues in the next verse.

For today: do not leave obedience for tomorrow. When you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word, respond today with a concrete step: forgiving, praying, correcting something, or trusting in him.
exp.7:9:
This verse says that God will make a new covenant with the house of Israel. The Berean Standard Bible uses the word "covenant" here, meaning a binding agreement that God Himself sets in place. Instead of laws written only on stone tablets, God says He will put His laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. In this way there will be a close relationship: He will be their God, and they will be His people.

The author of Hebrews quotes here the promise from Jeremiah 31:31-34. He writes to Christians of Jewish background to show that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant. The earlier context recalls that the covenant at Sinai was broken because of the people's unfaithfulness. Christians understand that this new covenant is fulfilled in Christ, although some debate how it relates to the future of Israel.

For today: obedience to God does not come from outside pressure, but from a heart that He transforms. Ask Him that you not only know His Word, but love it and live it from the inside.
exp.9:18:
The explanation says that believers, whom the author calls "brothers," now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place, that is, the place where God himself is present. Confidence here means assurance and courage, not fear. And this entrance is possible by the blood of Jesus Christ, that is, through his death offered on our behalf.

The author of Hebrews (tradition is not unanimous about his name) has just explained that God forgave sins under the new covenant and that no more sacrifices are needed. With "Therefore" he moves from teaching to application: if forgiveness is complete, we can approach God without dread. Before, only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, and only once a year.

For today: when you feel unworthy or far from God, pray with confidence. Your access does not depend on your performance, but on what Christ has done for you.
exp.5:4:
This verse continues to describe people who have had real experiences with God. "Who have tasted the goodness of the word of God" means they tested and came to know his message up close. "The powers of the coming age" refers to the powers of the future, that is, the displays of God's power that point ahead to the world he will bring.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to tired believers who may have been tempted to abandon Christ. He warns them seriously about the danger of turning away. Christians have understood this passage in different ways: some see a real loss of salvation, others see a description of people who seemed to believe but did not have true faith.

For today: do not be content with having tasted the things of God. Feed your faith every day with the Bible, prayer, and fellowship with other believers.
exp.9:4:
This verse says that Christ, when he came into the world, spoke to God the Father. He said that God did not desire sacrifice and offering, but that God had prepared a body for him. The word "prepared" in the verse is the one used here for what God did.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40:6-8 and places it on the lips of Jesus. He has just explained that the blood of animals cannot take away sins, and that those sacrifices only reminded people of their sins each year. So God prepared another way: a human body for Christ, who would offer himself in obedience. It should be noted that Hebrews here follows the ancient Greek version of the Psalm, which says "body," while the Hebrew text of the Psalm says something different ("you have opened my ears"). Scholars explain this in several ways.

God does not seek empty rituals, but obedient hearts. Today, instead of trusting in keeping religious duties, we can trust in what Christ did for us and respond to him with sincere obedience.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the first covenant, the one God made with Israel through Moses, had a fault. If it had been without fault, there would have been no reason to look for another. The word "fault" means a defect or flaw, and the second half of the verse says that no place would have been sought for a second covenant.

The author of Hebrews wrote to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to return to the old law. He shows them that Christ is the mediator of a better covenant. He then quotes the prophet Jeremiah, who had already spoken of a new covenant. The fault lay in the people's failure to remain faithful, not in any failure on God's part.

For today: do not trust your own efforts to be perfect before God. Rest in Christ, who gives you a new heart and complete forgiveness. Obey God out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.7:11:
God promises that he will forgive the wrongdoing of his people. To forgive means to release someone from guilt and be ready to show compassion. He says that their sins and their iniquities he will not remember anymore, that is, he will not hold them against them to punish them, nor will he bring them up against them again.

The author of Hebrews quotes the prophecy of Jeremiah 31 about the new covenant. He writes to believers of Jewish background to show them that Christ brings something better than the old covenant. This verse is the foundation for the promises before it: God writes his law on the heart, and everyone knows him, because forgiveness comes first. That God will not remember their sins does not mean he forgets, but that he decides not to count that sin against us any longer.

Today, if you have trusted in Christ, do not live bound by guilt that has already been forgiven. Come before God with confidence, confess whatever weighs on you, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.3:6:
God again marked out a certain day, calling it "today." He did this a long time later, speaking through David, as the verse says: "Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts." The phrase "designated" means that God fixes or sets apart a specific time. "If you hear" is an invitation to listen, and "do not harden your hearts" is a warning against becoming stubborn. The point is to listen to God with an open heart.

The author of Hebrews writes to Jewish believers and quotes Psalm 95, which David wrote centuries after the people of Israel failed in the wilderness. His argument is that if God was still saying "today" in David's time, the promise of rest had not run out. There was still an opportunity to enter it.

For today: do not put off what God is showing you. When you sense that He is speaking to you through His Word, respond today with humility and obedience, before your heart gets used to saying "no."
exp.10:27:
He says that Moses, by faith, kept the Passover and commanded that the blood of the lamb be sprinkled. The sprinkling of the blood refers to that blood placed on the doorposts. "The destroyer of the firstborn" is the destroyer sent in the last plague on Egypt. Because of that sign, Israel's firstborn were not touched.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, encourages believers who were under pressure and temptation to turn back. He gives them examples of faith, and here shows Moses trusting in God's word, even though he did not yet see the result. After the Passover come the crossing of the sea and the fall of Jericho. Many Christians see in the lamb's blood a picture of Christ.

Today, faith is not only feeling confident but obeying what God says. Think of a step of obedience you have put off, and take it today, trusting in his promise.
exp.9:38:
The verse says that believers are not among those who shrink back and are destroyed, but among those who have faith and preserve their souls. "Shrinking back" means turning away or giving up. "Destroyed" means being completely ruined. To preserve the soul means to keep it safe and secure. "Faith" here refers to trusting God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were under pressure and mistreatment because of their faith. There was a risk that they would turn back. He quotes the prophet Habakkuk: the righteous shall live by faith, and God is not pleased with the one who shrinks back. Then he encourages his readers with confidence: they are not part of that group.

For today: when you grow tired or trials make you doubt, do not keep going on your own strength alone. Seek God in prayer, read his Word, and lean on brothers and sisters who encourage you. A small step of faith today helps you stay firm.
exp.2:17:
To whom did God swear that they would never enter His rest? The answer is: to those who disobeyed. "Swore" means that God made a solemn promise, in this case a serious warning. The "rest" was the promised land, where the people would find relief from their journey through the wilderness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to give up. He reminds them of what happened to Israel after leaving Egypt. Many heard God, but they hardened their hearts. The following verse explains that they did not enter because of unbelief, and that lack of trust showed itself in disobedience.

For today: true faith trusts God and shows itself in obeying him. Today, if God speaks to you through his Word, do not harden your heart; take a concrete step of obedience.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that every house has someone who built it, and that God is the builder of everything. The word translated here as "built" simply means "made." Here "house" is not only a building but the people or family of God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who felt pressure to turn back. He compares Moses, who was highly respected, with Jesus. Moses was faithful in God's house, but Jesus is the builder. Many understand that by saying God built everything, the author presents Christ with divine dignity.

For today: if God is the one who builds his house, your life and your faith rest in him, not in your own strength. Remain firm in trust and hope, even in difficult times.
exp.9:14:
The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this. This verse says that the Holy Spirit bears witness to us about what the author has just explained. The Spirit's testimony is what confirms it for us. Then the text introduces a quotation from Scripture with the words "First He says," and the quotation continues in the following verses.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, writes to believers of Jewish background. He explains that Christ's sacrifice was sufficient and complete. To support this, he quotes the promise of the new covenant from Jeremiah 31, and he says that the Holy Spirit speaks through those ancient words.

For today: when you doubt that God has truly forgiven you, return to what his Word says. The Spirit testifies that Christ's work is enough, and you can rest in that promise without trying to earn forgiveness.
exp.6:19:
The explanation says that Jesus's priesthood was not established without God making an oath. The verse's wording points to "none of this happened without an oath," and the sentence is finished in the next verse: the other priests became priests without an oath, but Jesus was made priest with one.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior to the Levitical priesthood. He quotes Psalm 110:4, where God swears that his priest will be one forever. An oath from God shows that his decision is firm and definitive.

For today: you can rest in the fact that your relationship with God through Jesus does not depend on your strength or your steadiness, but on a firm promise that God upholds. When you doubt, remember that He committed Himself with an oath.
exp.10:21:
It says that Joseph, when his end was near, trusted that God would keep his promise to bring Israel out of Egypt. The word "exodus" in the verse refers to the people's leaving. The phrase "gave instructions" means that he gave a clear request: that his bones be carried with them to the promised land.

The writer of Hebrews goes through examples of faith from the Old Testament. Joseph lived in Egypt as a ruler, but he did not cling to that place. According to Genesis 50:24-25, he trusted that God would visit his people. Later, Exodus 13:19 tells that Moses carried his bones. The text gives no further details about how Joseph understood all of this.

For today: faith not only helps us live in the present, it also looks ahead with confidence in God's promises. Even if you have comfort or success here, remember that your final hope is in God. Live and plan in such a way that your decisions show that confidence.
exp.11:13:
It says we should eagerly pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness. "Pursue" means to go after something with effort, to strive to reach it. "Holiness" means living set apart for God, with a clean life given over to Him. The text says that without it, no one will see the Lord.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who are worn down by hardship. He urges them to lift their drooping hands and walk with steady steps so that the weak among them may be healed. Then he warns them against bitterness and against living like Esau, who gave up what was valuable for a bowl of food. Christians understand this holiness in different ways: as the fruit of Christ's work, as a path of growth, or as both.

Today we can take one concrete step: ask forgiveness from someone, or forgive someone, and pray that God will make us more like Jesus.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that when sins have already been forgiven, an offering to deal with them is no longer needed. "Forgiven" here means completely pardoned, and "offering for sin" is the sacrifice that was once brought to seek that pardon.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whose identity is debated, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He has just quoted Jeremiah's promise about the new covenant, where God says he will remember their sins no more. His argument is that Jesus' sacrifice fulfilled that promise, so the repeated sacrifices in the temple are no longer necessary.

For today: if you have trusted in Christ, you do not have to live trying to earn forgiveness through your own efforts, guilt, or punishments. When you fail, come to God with sincerity and gratitude, not with fear, because Jesus has already paid what was necessary.
exp.11:1:
While we run the race of faith, the verse tells us to keep our eyes fixed on Jesus. He is the "author," the one who begins our faith, and the "perfecter," the one who brings it to its goal. For the joy set before him, he endured the cross and scorned its shame. Today he is seated at the right hand of God's throne.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself, and his name is not known with certainty. He writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up because of pressure and suffering. Earlier he mentions the heroes of faith in chapter 11, and now he points to Jesus as the greatest example.

When you feel exhausted or ashamed for following Christ, do not look only at your problems. Set aside a moment each day to think about what Jesus suffered and about the hope he had. That renews your strength to keep going forward.
exp.9:29:
This verse reminds us that God is the one who carries out justice. The author quotes two phrases from the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:35-36): "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay" and "The Lord will judge His people." In these words, repayment means the fair response of God to what each person has done, the justice that puts wrong right.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon Christ because of pressure and suffering. He warns them that turning away from Jesus, after knowing the truth, is something very serious. God judges with justice, even his own people.

For today: when someone hurts you, do not take revenge; leave justice to God. At the same time, live with seriousness and gratitude the faith you received, without taking lightly what Christ did for you.
exp.10:36:
Many believers suffered terrible things for their faith. They were stoned, sawed in two, or put to death by the sword. The word "tempted" in this verse most likely means they were put to the test, perhaps pressed to give up their faith. Others went around wrapped in sheepskins and goatskins, with no secure home, poor, oppressed, and mistreated.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whose identity we do not know for certain, writes to tired believers who were under pressure. In chapter 11 he goes through a list of heroes of the faith. Here he shows that faith does not always bring immediate relief; sometimes it costs a great deal. Even so, the text that follows says the world was not worthy of them.

Today, if your faith brings you mockery, loneliness or hardship, do not think God has abandoned you. Remember that others have walked that road and God counted them as precious. Keep trusting, one day at a time.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that Christ did not take the glory of becoming high priest on himself. It was God who called him, saying to him: "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father." The phrase "high priest" means the chief priest. The wording about being a son speaks of the Son's unique relationship with the Father, and the passage it draws on is Psalm 2:7.

The writer of Hebrews explains that no one appoints himself to the priesthood, as Aaron was not self-appointed either. God calls the priest. In this way the writer shows that Jesus is a legitimate priest, since his office comes from God and not from his own ambition. Who wrote Hebrews is not known with certainty, but the message is addressed to believers with a Jewish background.
