For today: Jesus did not seek his own honor, but obeyed the Father's call. We can ask God to teach us to serve without seeking applause, trusting that his calling and his approval are worth more than any human recognition.
exp.7:12:
By speaking of a "new covenant," God has made the first one obsolete. What is obsolete and aging will soon disappear.

The writer of Hebrews addresses believers with a Jewish background. He has just quoted the promise from Jeremiah 31 about a covenant in which everyone would know God and their sins would be forgiven. His argument is that God himself announced something new, and this shows that the first covenant was not the final stage of the plan. Scholars debate how to connect this with the destruction of the temple in the year 70, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today we can rest in Christ, not in our achievements or rituals. If God promises forgiveness and a close relationship, we can come to him with confidence, without fear that our past will disqualify us.
exp.8:0:
This verse says that the first covenant, the one God made with Israel, had rules for worship and an earthly sanctuary. The word "Now" simply introduces what follows, meaning "then" or "at this point." The "regulations for worship" are the instructions about how to worship God. "Earthly" here does not mean sinful, but belonging to this present world, made of visible materials.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Christ is better than the old system. Before he speaks of Jesus as high priest, he describes the tabernacle, which was a shadow of something greater.

For today: rituals and sacred places can help us, but they are not the center. Today we can approach God with confidence through Jesus. Ask yourself whether your faith rests on religious customs or on a living relationship with Christ.
exp.0:6:
The verse says that God makes his angels winds, and his servants flames of fire. Winds and flames are both powerful and quick, which shows that the angels are strong, but their role is to serve.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, quotes Psalm 104:4 here. He writes to believers with a Jewish background and wants to show that Jesus is superior to the angels. The angels are servants of God, but the next verse says that the Son is called God and is given an eternal throne.

Today, this text invites us to put Jesus first. The angels are a gift from God, but only Christ deserves our worship and trust.
exp.11:21:
This verse says that believers in Christ are no longer standing before a terrifying mountain, as Israel did at Sinai, but have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God. There is the heavenly Jerusalem and a vast gathering of angels, myriads of them. "Have come" means that they have drawn near. "Myriads" means countless thousands, a very large multitude.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. He compares the fear of Sinai, where even Moses trembled, with the privilege of drawing near to God through Jesus. Many understand the heavenly city to be the spiritual reality to which we already have access.

For today: when you feel that God is distant or that your faith is small, remember that Christ opened the way for you. Pray with reverence, but with confidence, because you have been invited into his presence.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that Jesus, unlike other priests, lives forever. That is why his priesthood is "permanent": it does not end or pass to someone else. The word "because" points to the reason for the contrast, and "lives forever" means that he remains alive and faithful.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known with certainty, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares Jesus with the priests of the Old Testament, who were many because death kept them from continuing to serve. Jesus, by contrast, rose again, and so his service never comes to an end. This supports the idea that he guarantees a better covenant.

Today we can rest in the fact that our relationship with God does not depend on people who fail or die, but on Christ, who is always present. When you feel weak or guilty, draw near to God with confidence and pray in the name of Jesus.
exp.9:15:
This verse speaks of a new covenant that God promises. Instead of laws written only on stone or in a book, God says he will put his laws in people's hearts and inscribe them on their minds. The phrase "after those days" refers to the time that comes after the old covenant.

The writer of Hebrews quotes the prophecy of Jeremiah 31:33 and points out that the Holy Spirit bears witness through that Scripture. His purpose is to show that Christ's sacrifice, offered only once, accomplished what the repeated offerings of the temple could not: complete forgiveness and a transformation from within.

For today: do not live your faith only as a list of rules you keep out of obligation. Ask God to shape your desires and your way of thinking himself. Read his Word with confidence, knowing that you are already forgiven and that his Spirit helps you obey with love.
exp.2:12:
It says that believers should encourage and warn one another every day, for as long as it can still be called "today." The purpose is that none of them be hardened, that is, that none become numb to God, deceived by sin. The verb rendered here as "exhort" means to encourage, advise, and urge. The word "but" is not needed in this verse; the sentence simply continues the thought.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to Jewish Christians who were tempted to turn away from Christ. He quotes Psalm 95 and reminds his readers of the people of Israel in the wilderness, who did not trust God and did not enter his rest. He warns them that unbelief begins gradually.

For today: seek out a brother or sister in the faith and this week encourage them with a word or a message, and pray with them. Also allow someone you trust to speak to you honestly.
exp.2:7:
This verse asks us not to close our hearts to God. "Harden" means becoming stubborn and unwilling to listen. "Rebellion" is the defiance that angers God, and "testing" here means that the people challenged God, doubting him. The "wilderness" recalls the time when Israel walked toward the promised land.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95 and says that it is the Holy Spirit who speaks. He writes to believers who could grow weary and turn back. He reminds them that the people of Israel, even after seeing the works of God, rebelled in the wilderness. It is a warning not to repeat that story and to stay firm in Christ.

For today: when you sense that God is speaking to you through his Word, do not put it off for later. Respond with humility and obedience today, even if you are tired or doubting. A soft heart allows itself to be guided.
exp.2:5:
He says that Christ is faithful as a Son over God's house, not as a servant. That house is us, that is, God's people, on one condition: that we hold firmly to our confidence and to the hope we boast about. The phrase "hold firmly" means to keep hold of what we have been given, and the "hope we boast about" refers to the hope in which we take joy.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background who felt tempted to give up their faith under pressure. He compares Moses, faithful as a servant, with Christ, faithful as a Son. Then, using the example of the wilderness, he encourages them not to harden their hearts.

For today: when tiredness or doubt comes, do not trust in your own strength. Seek Christ in prayer, in the Bible, and in the company of other believers, so that you may stay firm in the hope.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that somewhere in Scripture the seventh day is spoken of, and that on that day God rested from all his works. The words "somewhere" refer to a passage the author quotes, in this case Genesis 2:2. The word "rested" means that God stopped his work of creation because it was already finished.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to give up their faith. He uses God's rest in creation to show that the rest he promises was already prepared from the beginning. He wants his readers not to be like the Israelites in the wilderness, who heard the promise but did not receive it with faith.

For today: God invites you to rest in what Christ has already done, without trying to earn his favor by your own effort. Today you can hand him one specific worry and trust that he cares for you.
exp.12:4:
This verse asks that the way we live not be marked by the love of money, that is, by the desire to always have more. Instead, we should be content with what we have now. The reason is a promise from God: "Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you," which means that he will never abandon us.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers who had suffered pressure and losses because of their faith. Shortly before, he speaks of love for one another, of caring for prisoners, and of faithfulness in marriage. Here he adds the subject of money, and he supports his advice with an ancient promise that God gave to his people in the Old Testament.

Today, before buying something on impulse or envying what belongs to others, we can stop and give thanks for what we already have, remembering that our security is in God.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that nothing in all creation is hidden from God. Everything is uncovered and exposed before his eyes, with nothing to cover it. It also says that we will have to give an account to him, that is, answer for our lives. The phrase "nothing in all creation" means any created thing at all. The word "exposed" means plainly open to view.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to give up. Using the example of the people in the wilderness, he warns them not to harden their hearts. God's word reveals the deepest part of us, and this God who sees everything is also the one who receives us through Jesus, our great High Priest.

Today we can stop pretending before God. Since he already knows everything, we can pray with sincerity, confess our failings, and draw near with confidence, because Jesus understands us.
exp.8:16:
A will is a document that passes an inheritance from one person to another. The person who makes the will is the one who leaves the inheritance. The verse says that a will takes effect only after the person who made it has died. While that person is still alive, what they promised cannot yet be claimed.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that the death of Christ was necessary so that those who are called might receive the eternal inheritance. The Greek word here can mean either "covenant" or "will," and scholars debate whether the author plays on both meanings.

Today you can receive forgiveness and eternal life as a gift, not as a wage. Rest in what Christ has already done, and let that lead you to thank him every day.
exp.5:17:
He tells us that God gives us a very strong encouragement based on "two things that cannot change," that is, his promise and his oath. It is impossible for God to lie. This encourages those who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not stated and whose identity is debated, writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up their faith. He reminds them that God made a promise to Abraham and confirmed that promise with an oath. In this way he wants to give them assurance that their hope in Christ is not fragile.

For today: when you feel doubt or fear, do not rely on your feelings, which change. Take a promise of God, read it aloud, and pray with it, holding on to it as to a firm rope.
exp.10:32:
This verse speaks of people who, trusting in God, accomplished great things. "Conquered kingdoms" means they won victories over nations and territories. "Administered justice" means they ruled and judged fairly, and "gained what was promised" means they saw fulfilled what God had promised. "Shut the mouths of lions" recalls that God protected some of them from being devoured.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were tired and pressed by suffering. He has just named Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel. Many think "shut the mouths of lions" alludes to Daniel, though it may also refer to Samson or David. His purpose is to encourage perseverance by showing examples of faith.

Today you can remember that faith is not an abstract idea, but trust that shows itself in brave and upright decisions. Ask God for faith to obey him today in something concrete, even if it frightens you.
exp.12:9:
We Christians, the explanation says, have an altar of our own, meaning a sacrifice and an offering that belong to us. Those who keep serving at the tabernacle have no right to eat from it. "Right" means permission or entitlement. The tabernacle was the place of worship in the Old Testament.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to return to laws about food and rituals. Earlier he had urged them not to be carried away by strange teachings. Many understand the altar to refer to Christ and his cross; others think of a broader idea of Christ's work. The verses that follow connect it with Jesus, who suffered outside the gate.

Today, do not look for your spiritual security in rituals, rules, or practices added to Christ. Rest in his complete sacrifice, and let his grace steady your heart.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that Christ, when he came into the world, presented himself before God with complete willingness: "Here I am, I have come to do your will." With that, he takes away the first, that is, he sets aside the animal sacrifices of the law, so that he may establish the second, that is, the last: God's will carried out in Christ.

The author of Hebrews quotes Psalm 40 and applies it to Jesus. He writes to believers of Jewish background who valued the temple sacrifices very highly. He wants to show them that those sacrifices pointed to something greater and could not remove sin completely. Jesus, through his obedience and the offering of his body, opened a new and final way.

For today: we do not have to earn forgiveness through religious effort. Rest in what Christ has already done, and respond as he did, saying to God each day: "Here I am, let your will be done."
exp.3:0:
We should take this seriously and be careful. God's offer to enter his rest still stands, and no one should be left outside it. The phrase "be deemed to have fallen short" means that someone is found to have been left behind, without reaching it. The word "you" in this verse is plural, addressed to all of you.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to believers of Jewish origin. He has just reminded them of Israel in the wilderness, who did not enter the rest because of their unbelief. He warns them not to repeat that mistake. It is debated whether the "rest" refers mainly to the Promised Land, to rest in Christ, or to future rest with God; the text seems to join these ideas together.

Today, do not take your faith for granted. Make time to listen to the Word and respond to it with trust and obedience, not just with your ears.
exp.12:15:
This verse calls us not to neglect doing good and sharing what we have with others. Here "sharing" means giving, being generous, and standing with others, especially those in need, rather than simply chatting. It says that God is pleased with such sacrifices, that is, with gifts made out of ordinary daily life.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who live under pressure. He has just spoken of the sacrifice of praise, and now he adds that worship is also shown through deeds. Since we do not have a lasting city here, we can live with open hands.

Today, you could look this week for someone with a specific need, a neighbor, a relative, or someone in your church, and help them with your time, your food, or your money. Do it as worship to God.
exp.5:7:
The passage describes a field that receives rain and yet produces only thorns and thistles. Such land is worthless. Its curse is near, and in the end it will be burned, as a field full of weeds is cleared.

The author of Hebrews was writing to believers who were at risk of turning away from Christ. He uses the image of the field: the same rain falls on the whole land, but the fruit shows the difference. Christians interpret this passage in various ways: some see a warning about losing salvation, others about a faith that was never genuine. Even so, the author quickly encourages his readers with hope.

Today it invites us to ask ourselves what fruit we are producing with everything God has given us. We can ask him to help us grow in love and faithfulness, and not to take his grace lightly.
exp.9:34:
This verse urges us not to let go of our confidence in God. The phrase "it holds a great reward" makes clear that this confidence is worth a great deal, and God will reward it. Put simply: do not throw away your faith, because it is worth a great deal and God will reward it.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who had already suffered mockery, imprisonment, and the loss of their possessions, and who had been sustained by the joy of hoping for something better. Now they may have been growing weary. He reminds them of their past courage to encourage them to remain steadfast until what was promised arrives.

Today, when you grow tired of waiting or of doing good without seeing results, remember how God sustained you before. Write down one time he helped you and return to that memory. Trust him for one more day.
exp.9:23:
It says we should pay close attention to one another, that is, think about the good of others and not only about ourselves. The purpose is to spur one another on, to encourage each other so that we grow in love and in good deeds.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background who were facing pressure and weariness. After explaining that Christ is our high priest and opens the way to God for us, he invites them to draw near with faith, to hold firmly to hope, and to care for one another. The next verse urges them not to give up meeting together.

For today: think of someone in your church or close circle and encourage them this week with a message, a visit, or a concrete help. In this way love becomes action.
exp.6:25:
This verse says that Jesus is the high priest we truly needed. The phrase "high priest" appears in the verse itself. He is described as holy, meaning completely devoted to God; innocent, free from wrongdoing; and undefiled, without any stain. He is "set apart from sinners," which does not mean that he looked down on them, but that he is different from them because he has no sin. And he is "exalted above the heavens," meaning he has been raised to a supreme place.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior to the priests of the old covenant, who were weak and needed to offer sacrifices for their own sins.

For today: because Jesus is perfect and lives interceding for us, we can approach God with confidence, without fear, even after we have failed.
exp.5:19:
He says that Jesus has entered on our behalf as the one who goes ahead, into the place where our hope reaches: the presence of God. The one who goes ahead opens the way so that others can follow. A high priest is the one who presents the people before God. "Forever" means without end. His priesthood is of a different kind from Aaron's, not based on family inheritance and not ended by death.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers who were at risk of losing heart. He has just spoken of hope as an anchor of the soul, and now he shows where that anchor is fastened: in Jesus, who has already entered the heavenly sanctuary. Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14 and in Psalm 110.

For today: when you feel shaken by uncertainty, remember that your hope does not depend on your own strength. Jesus has already reached where you are going, and he prays for you. Rest in him and speak with God with confidence.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that Jesus does not come to help the angels, but the descendants of Abraham. The word "helps" here means to take someone by the hand to aid and rescue them. The "descendants of Abraham" are the people who share in the faith that Abraham had.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus truly became human, with flesh and blood, to defeat death and free those who lived in fear. That is why he can be a compassionate high priest.

When you feel that no one understands your struggle or your fear, remember that Jesus became one of us. He knows temptation and pain from experience, and He helps you up close. Draw near to Him in prayer with confidence.
exp.9:6:
It says that someone presents himself to God with complete readiness: "Here I am, I have come to do your will." The phrase "it is written about me in the scroll" refers to what the Scriptures had already said about him. "Here I am" expresses his readiness to be present and to act.

The author of Hebrews puts these words in the mouth of Christ as he comes into the world. He quotes Psalm 40:6-8 to show that animal sacrifices were not the final purpose; God wanted obedience from the heart. Christ offers himself, and so the new replaces the old. Some understand "the scroll" to mean the whole Old Testament; others, a particular passage.

For today: Jesus shows us that what God seeks is a willing heart. Today you can simply say to him, "Here I am, Lord," and obey him in something concrete this day.
exp.1:9:
It was fitting for God, for whom and through whom all things exist, to make Jesus, the author of our salvation, perfect through suffering. Jesus is the one who opens the way to our salvation and begins it. In this way God would bring many sons to glory. "Perfect" means brought to fullness, complete in his mission; it does not mean that Jesus had any sin to be corrected.

The author of Hebrews (no one knows for certain who he was) writes to believers tempted to abandon their faith. He has just spoken of Jesus, made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honor because he suffered. He explains that the cross was not a failure but the path God chose. The next verse says that Jesus calls us brothers.

For today: when you suffer, remember that Jesus has already walked that road and does not leave you alone. Your pain does not mean God has forgotten you; it can draw you closer to the One who leads you to his glory.
exp.9:36:
It says that there is only a very short time left before the One who is coming arrives, and that when he comes he will not delay. "In just a little while" means "within a very short time." "He who is coming" refers to the Messiah, that is, to Christ, who is returning.

The writer of Hebrews is writing to believers who were tired, who had endured mockery and losses for following Jesus (Hebrews 10:32-34). He wants to encourage them not to give up. He quotes the book of Habakkuk, and no one knows for certain who wrote Hebrews. The idea of "will not delay" is understood from God's perspective, for whom time is not measured as it is for us.

For today: when the waiting feels long and you grow weary of doing good, remember that God keeps what he promises. Keep trusting him, pray, and remain faithful today, even if you do not yet see the result.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that the rules of the old system of worship concerned food and drink and special washings. They were external regulations, outward matters of the body rather than matters of the heart. The verse calls them rules imposed until the time of reform, meaning the time when God would set things right and bring them to their proper end.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the tabernacle and its rites pointed toward something greater. They were temporary, until Christ came and fulfilled what they announced.

Today we can remember that no ritual or religious effort cleanses our conscience by itself. If you feel guilty or believe you must earn forgiveness, rest in Christ, whose sacrifice did reach far enough, forever. Obey God, but out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.7:0:
The main point of everything the author has explained so far is this: we have a high priest who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven. The phrase "point of what we are saying" means the summary or central idea. Sitting "at the right hand" is a place of honor and authority.

Hebrews is a letter of unknown authorship; several names have been suggested, but none is certain. It was written to believers with a Jewish background who were tempted to return to their former practices. The author shows them that Jesus is better than the priests of the temple, because he serves in heaven, in the true sanctuary.

For today: if Jesus is seated beside God, your prayer does not go unattended. You can approach God with confidence, without fear, knowing that someone with authority and compassion intercedes for you.
exp.2:0:
This verse invites believers, whom God has set apart for himself and so calls "holy brothers," to set their focus on Jesus. It presents him as the apostle, the one sent from God, and as the high priest, the one who brings people near to God. The phrase "the heavenly calling" refers to God's call that comes from heaven, and "whom we confess" means the faith that believers openly affirm.

The writer of Hebrews does not name himself in the text, and people have debated who he was. He writes to believers of Jewish background who may have been tempted to give up their faith. He then compares Jesus with Moses, whom they respected greatly, and shows that Jesus is greater, just as the builder is greater than the house.

For today: when you feel tired or doubtful, do not first look to your own strength or your problems. Set aside a few minutes each day to read about Jesus in the Gospels and to pray, remembering that he represents you before God.
exp.10:14:
The explanation says that if those believers had kept thinking fondly about the land they had left, they would have had many chances to go back. The phrase "they really had the time" means they truly had the opportunity. But they did not return.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, speaks of Abraham, Sarah, and other patriarchs. He wants to encourage weary believers to stay firm. These men and women lived as strangers, and their eyes were fixed on what God had promised them, not on the country they had left behind. That is why, the text says, God is not ashamed to be called their God.

For today: when following God becomes hard, do not keep looking back longingly at what you left. Ask him to fix your heart on his promises, and take one concrete step of faithfulness today, even if you do not yet see the result.
exp.12:21:
I urge you, brothers, to bear with this message of encouragement and warning. The author asks his readers, whom he calls brothers, to hear what he has written with patience. "Bear with" means to receive it with a willing attitude, and a "word of exhortation" is a message that both encourages and warns. "I have only written to you briefly" means the letter was short and did not go on at length.

The book of Hebrews does not name its author, and we cannot be certain who he was. It speaks to Christians of Jewish background who were tempted to give up and turn back. The whole letter shows that Jesus is superior to everything. Here the author closes warmly, asking for openness, right after a blessing and just before mentioning Timothy.

For today: when someone tells you a Bible truth that makes you uncomfortable, do not get defensive right away. Listen with humility, pray, and ask God what he wants to change in you.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that Jesus had to become like us, his brothers, in every way. In this way he could be a compassionate and faithful high priest in service to God. The phrase "high priest" refers to the chief priest, and "atonement" means the covering or removal of sin through a sacrifice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that Jesus became human, a descendant of Abraham, to free us from the fear of death. Because he himself suffered and was tempted, he understands our struggles and can help us.

For today: when you feel alone, tired, or tempted, remember that Jesus truly understands you. Speak to him with confidence in prayer, without pretending or hiding, because he is compassionate and offers you forgiveness and help.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that Jesus is not a distant or indifferent high priest. A high priest is the one who brings people before God. The word "weaknesses" refers to our frailties and struggles. Jesus understands what we feel, because he was tempted in every way that we are, yet he never sinned.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers who needed encouragement not to abandon their faith. Earlier he spoke of God seeing everything, and of Jesus having entered heaven. That is why this verse brings comfort: this Jesus, so great, also understands us. The verses that follow invite us to draw near with confidence.

Today, when you feel weak, tired, or tempted, do not hide from God out of shame. Speak to him honestly, knowing that Jesus understands you and offers you mercy and help in time of need.
exp.9:13:
It says that Jesus, through one offering (his death on the cross), accomplished something complete and lasting. The phrase "made perfect" means that he brought them to their goal, making them ready to stand before God. "Those who are being sanctified" refers to those who have been set apart for God.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known with certainty, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares the temple sacrifices, which were always being repeated, with Christ's single sacrifice. He wants to encourage them not to turn back. Then he quotes the new covenant, where God writes his law on the heart.

For today: if you trust in Christ, your relationship with God does not depend on your efforts or on starting over each day. Rest in what he has already done, and live thankful, letting God keep transforming your heart.
exp.10:2:
Through faith, it says, we understand that the universe was formed at God's command. "The universe" here covers everything that was created. "Formed" means put in order or prepared. What we see was not made out of anything visible. It came from God's command, which no one could see.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who needed to keep going. After defining faith, he begins a list of witnesses from the past. First he mentions creation, something no one witnessed, which is accepted by trusting God. Then come Abel, Enoch, and others.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that the God who formed everything by his command is still at work even when you cannot see it. Trust him today in a specific situation.
exp.9:32:
Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution, like someone put on a stage for everyone to see. Ridicule means mockery and insult, and persecution means severe suffering. At other times you stood with others who were going through the same things, meaning you did not keep yourselves apart from them.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were under pressure because of their faith and were tempted to give up. He asks them to remember the early days after they came to know Christ. He reminds them of their earlier steadfastness to encourage them not to lose their confidence.

For today: when someone suffers for their faith or through a trial, do not leave them alone. Standing with them through visits, prayer, or concrete help is a real way of loving, and it also strengthens your own trust in God.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that the Lord disciplines the people he loves. The word "disciplines" here means to train or correct, as a father does with his children. "Chastises" is a strong image for firm correction. "Every son He receives" means everyone whom God accepts as his own.

The author of Hebrews writes to Christians who were weary from hardships. He quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 to remind them that suffering does not mean God has abandoned them. On the contrary, many understand that God uses trials to shape them as a good father would. Interpreters debate which specific trials he had in mind, but the central message is clear.

For today: when you go through correction or difficulty, do not lose heart right away. Ask God what he wants to teach you, and trust that his dealings come from love, not rejection.
exp.12:19:
This verse begins a prayer of blessing. It calls God "the God of peace," the one who brought our Lord Jesus back from the dead, and it calls Jesus "the great Shepherd of the sheep." This happened through the blood of the eternal covenant, that is, through the blood of the covenant or agreement that lasts forever.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, closes his letter with a prayer for his readers. Earlier he asked them to pray for him. Throughout the letter he has explained that Jesus established a new and better covenant. Here he sums up that teaching and asks that God strengthen them.

For today: when you feel tired or lost, remember that your shepherd lives and cares for you. You can pray with confidence, asking God to help you do his will, because he himself gives the strength to do it.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that what happened at Mount Sinai was so frightening that even Moses, the leader of the people, was filled with fear. "Terrifying" here means causing deep dread, not simply something bad. Saying "I am trembling with fear" points to a real trembling of the body, a sign of being overcome with dread.

The author of Hebrews compares two mountains. He recalls how Israel received the law amid trumpets, voices, and limits that no one could cross. This statement from Moses does not appear word for word in Exodus; it is thought that the author is recalling or summarizing a tradition, and scholars explain this in different ways. His purpose is to show that, before God, the people felt distant and afraid, so that he can then contrast this with the access we now have in Christ.

Today we can draw near to God with confidence through Jesus, without forgetting that he remains holy. Cultivate a sincere reverence when you pray and worship.
exp.2:10:
God, angry at the rebellion of his people, made a solemn oath: that generation would never enter his "rest." The word "swore" means that he promised something with complete seriousness, with an oath. "Rest" means peace, security, and quiet trust in God's presence.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 95, in which the Holy Spirit speaks and presents the words of God. He reminds us of the people of Israel in the desert, who doubted God and tested him for forty years, even while they saw his works. Because of their unbelief, that generation did not enter the promised land. The writer uses this as a warning for the believers of his own time. Interpreters explain in various ways how serious the warning is, but all agree that it calls us to persevere in faith.

Today, do not harden your heart. When God speaks to you through his Word, respond with trust and obedience, and seek the encouragement of other believers every day.
exp.1:7:
He says that God placed everything under the rule of human beings, so that nothing was left outside that rule. But the author admits a reality: we do not yet see everything made subject to humanity. "Placed everything under his feet" means that all things were put under his authority.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself in the text, quotes Psalm 8 to write to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, made human, fulfills what that psalm promises. Although today the world seems disordered, the next verse points to Jesus, crowned with glory after suffering death.

When life seems out of control, remember that Jesus is already crowned and that the end of history is in God's hands. You can wait with patience and confidence, praying and obeying today.
exp.9:25:
If someone sins on purpose after having come to know the truth of the gospel, no other sacrifice remains that can save them. "Deliberately going on sinning" describes sin that is done consciously and keeps going on; "no further sacrifice for sins remains" means that outside of Christ there is no other offering that forgives.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to abandon Christ and go back to their former practices. He has just encouraged them to meet together and to encourage one another. Then he warns them seriously: rejecting Christ knowingly leaves a person without hope, because his sacrifice is the only one. Christians interpret this warning in different ways: some see a total falling away, others a warning to examine one's faith.

Today, take sin seriously, but do not turn away from the church. Stay close to other believers, confess your failings, and come to Christ with humility.
exp.11:9:
Hebrews 12:10 says that our earthly fathers disciplined us for a short time, doing what seemed best to them, though they could be wrong. God, by contrast, disciplines us for our good, with a clear purpose: that we may share in his holiness. Here "disciplines" means training and guiding, not only punishment.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who were worn down by hardship and tempted to give up. He reminds them that difficulties do not mean God has abandoned them. On the contrary, they show that he treats them as his children and is shaping them.

Today, when you go through a hardship or a correction, do not ask only "Why me?" Also ask, "Lord, what do you want to teach me?" Trust that your Father does not discipline you out of anger, but out of love, to help you grow.
exp.2:2:
This verse says that Jesus has been counted worthy of greater honor than Moses, just as the builder of a house deserves more honor than the house itself. "Greater glory" here means greater honor, and "worthy" means deserving respect. Moses was highly respected, but Jesus holds a higher place.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and whom people have debated much, writes to Jewish believers who valued Moses greatly. He wants to encourage them not to turn back, showing them that Jesus is superior. The verses that follow say that God is the one who created everything, and that Moses was faithful as a servant.

Today we can ask ourselves: does Jesus hold first place in my life? We can admire good leaders and teachers, but only Christ deserves our deepest trust and worship.
exp.10:24:
Moses made a decision: he chose to suffer oppression together with God's people rather than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. "Suffer oppression" means to be mistreated or to endure hardship. "Fleeting enjoyment of sin" refers to pleasures that last only a short time. Moses saw that those pleasures were not worth the cost.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who faced pressure and suffering. He gives them examples of people of faith. Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, but he chose to identify with Israel, an enslaved people. The text says he did this by faith, trusting in the reward that God would give.

Today, obeying God sometimes costs us acceptance, advantages, or peace of mind. Before deciding, ask yourself: "Does this give me only a passing relief, or does it keep me faithful to God?" Trusting Him can help you choose what lasts.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that Scripture bears witness about Jesus: he is a priest forever, not for a limited time. The phrase "in the order of Melchizedek" means that his priesthood is of the same kind as Melchizedek's, and different from the priesthood of Levi. Here, the word "testified" means that the Bible affirms it.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, quotes Psalm 110:4 to show his readers, Christians of Jewish background, that Jesus is a priest by the power of an endless life, that is, a life that does not come to an end. For this reason his priesthood replaces the one under the law, which was weak.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus intercedes for us without growing weary or coming to an end. When you fail or feel that God is far away, come near with confidence in prayer, knowing that your priest lives forever.
exp.4:7:
He says that Jesus, although he was the Son, learned obedience from what he suffered. This does not mean that he had been disobedient before, but that he lived out obedience fully, even in pain. The word "consummated" in the following verse means "brought to its fullness" or "made perfect" in his mission.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who are tired and tempted to give up. He shows them that Jesus is the perfect priest because he understands human suffering. The previous verse recalls his anguished prayer, perhaps alluding to Gethsemane, though some interpret it more broadly.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not think that God is far away. Jesus knows that path. Ask him for help to obey him also in difficult moments, trusting that God can shape your character even through pain.
exp.10:20:
He says that Jacob, near death, blessed each of Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. The staff is a walking stick, and "leaned on" simply means resting his weight on it.

The detail about the staff comes from an ancient Greek translation of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew text can be read as "the head of the bed," which is why it is explained in more than one way.

The writer of Hebrews is giving examples of people who trusted God's promises even though they did not see them fulfilled. Jacob, weak and old, looked ahead and believed that God would keep his word with his descendants.

For today: faith does not fade with old age or weakness. Even at the end of life we can worship God and bless others, leaving them words of hope and trust in Him.
exp.8:7:
By this arrangement the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed while the first tabernacle was still standing. The first tabernacle, the outer part where the priests went in regularly, stood in the way, and the inner sanctuary, where God's presence was, remained closed to the people. Here "disclosed" means made known or opened.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians of Jewish background. He explains that the rituals of the tabernacle pointed to something greater. Only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year, and with blood. That showed that access to God was still limited.

For today: in Christ, the way is open. You can come near to God with confidence, not depending on rituals or go-betweens, but trusting in what Jesus has done for you.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that it was necessary for the copies of the things in the heavens, meaning the tabernacle and its objects, to be purified with the blood of animals. But the heavenly realities themselves needed something better: far better sacrifices. The word for the copies is the one the Berean Standard Bible renders as "copies," and the word for the heavenly things is the one rendered "heavenly things." The word "So" marks the conclusion drawn from what has just been said. The plural "sacrifices" probably points to the excellence of Christ's one sacrifice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that the tabernacle system was a shadow, and that Christ is the reality. For this reason he compares the ancient sacrifices with his own.

For today: you do not have to achieve your cleansing through effort or rituals. You can draw near to God with confidence, resting in what Christ has already done for you, and live with gratitude and simplicity.
exp.11:10:
No discipline feels enjoyable while we are going through it; it feels painful and sad. But over time it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace, a more upright life, for those who have been trained by it. Here "discipline" means training and correction, like the way a loving father guides his child. Those who have been trained by it are shaped through it, much like an athlete is shaped by regular practice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Christians worn down by trials. He compares God to a father who corrects his children out of love. Human parents do this for a short time and with mistakes; God does it for our good and to make us holy. That is why he then encourages them to lift their drooping hands and keep moving forward.

When you go through a hardship or a correction, do not stay only in the pain. Ask God, "What do you want to teach me?" Trust that he is shaping you, and keep walking with patience.
exp.9:11:
He says that Jesus, after offering himself once for all time as a sacrifice for sins, sat down at the right hand of God. The phrase "at the right hand" means "at the right side," a place of honor and authority. "For all time" means that this sacrifice lasts forever and never needs to be repeated.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers with a Jewish background, and we do not know for certain who he was. He compares the priests of the temple, who offered sacrifices every day without ever finishing the task, with Jesus, who completed the work. That is why he sits down: his work of forgiveness is finished.

Today you can rest in the fact that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts or on repeating rituals to earn God's favor. When guilt accuses you, remember that Christ has already done what was necessary. Come near to God with gratitude and confidence, not with fear.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that Jesus, during his earthly life, offered prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save him from death, and that he was heard because of his reverence. "Was heard" does not necessarily mean that he was spared from dying, and scholars understand it in several ways.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named, explains why Christ is a true priest. A good priest understands human weakness. Many think this refers to Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane, although the text does not say so clearly.

We can pray with complete sincerity, even in tears, because Jesus knows pain. And we can trust that God hears us, even when his answer is different from what we asked for.
exp.9:10:
This verse describes the work of the Jewish priests. Day after day they stood in the temple to serve and to offer again and again the same animal sacrifices. The word "minister" means serving in worship. "Taking away sins" means removing them completely, and according to the text, those sacrifices could never do that.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity we do not know for certain, compares the old system with the work of Christ. Earlier he quoted Psalm 40 to show that Jesus came to do God's will. The fact that the sacrifices had to be repeated was a sign that they did not finish the matter. The next verse shows the contrast: Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus has already done what was necessary for our forgiveness. We do not need to try to earn it through repeated efforts or feelings of guilt. We can come near to God with gratitude and confidence, and live in obedience as a response to that love.
exp.10:19:
It says that Isaac blessed his sons Jacob and Esau by trusting in God, not only in what he could see. His blessings spoke of the future: "the future" means the things that were going to happen.

The author of Hebrews goes through the history of earlier believers to show how faith led them to trust God's promises. Here he speaks of Isaac, already an old man, when he blessed his sons (Genesis 27). That story was complicated, with deception within the family, but the text highlights that Isaac believed God would carry out his plan later on, and so he spoke about what was to come.

For today: we can bless and encourage our children and loved ones with words that express hope in God. Even when we cannot see the whole future, we can trust that God continues to guide his story.
exp.10:25:
He says that Moses considered that suffering disgrace for the sake of Christ was worth more than all the treasures of Egypt. Your verse speaks of the "reproach of Christ," meaning the disgrace or shame that comes with belonging to him. Moses looked ahead, waiting for the reward that God would give.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who faced pressure and rejection. He presents Moses to them as an example of faith. Some understand "the reproach of Christ" to mean that Moses suffered a disgrace similar to Christ's, or that he joined the people who would bring forth the Messiah. Interpreters explain it in several ways.

For today: when being faithful to Christ costs you a friendship, an easy gain, or a certain respect, remember that God sees and rewards. Ask yourself what you are valuing most, and decide with your eyes fixed on what is eternal.
exp.8:21:
According to the law, nearly everything had to be purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there was no forgiveness. "Forgiveness" here means the pardon of sins, and "purified" means made clean so that a person could draw near to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He reminds them how Moses used blood to confirm the covenant with Israel. His purpose is to show that all of that pointed to something better: the sacrifice of Christ, who entered heaven itself on our behalf.

For today: we do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or guilt. Christ has already given his life for us. When you feel the weight of a wrong, come to God with confidence and gratitude, knowing that forgiveness has already been paid for.
exp.10:0:
Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This verse says that faith is like a firm foundation for what we still hope for, and a confident sure knowledge of what we cannot see with our eyes. The words "assurance" and "certainty" in the verse point to something solid and sure, and to confidence or conviction. In other words, faith gives us inner certainty about God's promises, even though we have not yet seen them fulfilled.

The author of Hebrews is not identified with certainty; several names have been proposed, but no one knows for sure. He writes to believers who are tired or tempted to give up, and he wants to encourage them to trust God. This verse opens the chapter of the heroes of faith: people from the Old Testament who trusted God without seeing everything fulfilled.

Today, when you face an uncertain situation, such as an illness, a debt, or a long wait, you can lean on what God has already promised and shown. Pray, and take the next step with confidence, even though you cannot see the whole path.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that when God presents his Firstborn to the world, he commands all the angels to worship him. "Firstborn" is a title of honor and authority; it does not mean that Jesus was created. "Worship him" means to give him honor and reverence.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior to the angels. The quotation seems to come from passages such as Deuteronomy 32:43 (in the ancient Greek version) or Psalm 97:7. Scholars do not agree on whether "when God brings" refers to his birth, his resurrection, or his return.

For today: if the angels worship Jesus, we too can do so. Give him first place today in your decisions and in your gratitude.
exp.2:14:
This verse repeats an invitation: if you hear God's voice today, do not harden your heart, as you did in the rebellion. "As it has been said" means "as it is still being said to us." "The rebellion" refers to the time when the people of Israel turned against God in the wilderness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, quotes Psalm 95 to encourage Jewish Christians who were tired and tempted to abandon their faith. He reminds them that the generation of Moses heard God, but many of them distrusted him. For this reason he asks them to encourage one another every day.

For today: do not put off your response to God. When you sense that he speaks to you through his Word or through your conscience, obey him that same day, and seek out a brother or sister in the faith who will encourage you to remain steadfast.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that God has not stayed silent. Long ago he spoke to our ancestors, the Israelites, the "fathers," through the prophets. He did so on many past occasions and in many different ways, such as messages, visions, and signs.

Hebrews does not say who wrote it; that is not known for certain. It is addressed to believers with a Jewish background who were tempted to abandon their faith. The author begins by recalling that God spoke in the past, and right away shows that his greatest word came through the Son.

For today: God still wants to communicate with you. Read the Gospels carefully, because there you hear his clearest voice in Jesus.
exp.10:18:
Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and so, in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death. The verse describes Abraham's confidence that God has the power to bring life out of death, and it presents Isaac's return as something like a picture of that greater reality.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not given in the text, points to Abraham's faith. God had promised Abraham descendants through Isaac, and then asked him to offer Isaac as a sacrifice (Genesis 22). Abraham trusted that God would keep his promise, even if that required a miracle as great as bringing Isaac back to life.

For today: when God asks you to trust him in the middle of something you do not understand, remember his character and his promises. You can obey one step at a time, believing that he is faithful and powerful, even though you cannot yet see how he will work things out.
exp.4:12:
Hebrews 5:13 says that whoever still lives on milk, that is, on the most basic teachings, is still an infant and has no experience with the message of righteousness, meaning the teaching about what is right and pleasing to God. Such a person is still a spiritual infant. "Inexperienced" means lacking practice or skill. "Lives on milk" describes someone who keeps feeding on that basic teaching.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, gently rebukes believers who had already been in the faith for some time but had not matured. They should have been teaching others, and they still needed to review the basics. He speaks to them about Christ as priest and wants to lead them to a firmer faith.

For today: do not settle for the basics. Devote steady time to reading the Bible, studying it, and putting it into practice, so that your faith grows and you can help others.
exp.10:17:
This verse explains why Abraham's test was so hard. God had told him, "Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned." The word "offspring" means descendants, that is, the children and future generations. God's promise depended on Isaac.

The writer of Hebrews is speaking to believers who needed to keep going, and he sets Abraham before them as an example of faith. He points back to what God said in Genesis. Abraham received a promise and then a command that seemed to contradict it: to offer Isaac. The verses that follow say that Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. In this way he trusted God, even without understanding how God would keep his word.

For today: when what God says seems not to fit with the life you are living, do not abandon your trust. Remember that God is faithful and can act where you see no way out. Keep obeying with humility and peace.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that Christ has already come as high priest of the good things that have arrived. He went through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, one not made by human hands and not part of this created world.

The author of Hebrews was writing to Christians with a Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old rituals. He shows them that those ceremonies, with their foods, washings and sacrifices, could not cleanse the conscience. They were a sign pointing toward something better. With Christ came the time of renewal. Scholars explain in various ways exactly what that tabernacle is, but they all agree that it refers to heaven, where Christ serves.

Today we can rest in the fact that Jesus has already completed the work. We do not need to carry guilt or earn forgiveness through religious effort; we can draw near to God with confidence.
exp.11:8:
Verse 9 says that if we respected our earthly fathers when they disciplined us, we should all the more submit ourselves to God, the Father of our spirits. The word "disciplined" here refers to those who trained and guided us, not only those who punished us. "Respected" means we honored them with deference. "Live" speaks of the true life that God gives.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who are tired from trials and pressure. He explains that difficulties may be the discipline of a Father who treats them as His children. He wants to encourage them not to give up. The verses that follow say this discipline seeks our good and produces the fruit of righteousness.

Today, when you go through a difficulty, do not ask only "Why is this happening to me?" but also "What is God wanting to teach me?" Pray with humility and obey what He shows you, trusting that He disciplines you with love.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that the people of Israel were unable to enter the promised land, here called "his rest," for one clear reason: they did not believe. The phrase "because of" means "on account of" or "by reason of," and the wording "it was because of their unbelief" points to the same cause. The unbelief here is not just doubt, but not trusting God, and that led to not obeying him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to give up. He reminds them of what happened to the generation that left Egypt with Moses and fell in the wilderness. He quotes Psalm 95 to warn them not to repeat that mistake.

Today we can ask ourselves in what area we are distrusting God. When he asks something of us and we feel afraid, faith shows itself by taking the next step of obedience, even a small one, trusting that he keeps what he promises.
exp.11:15:
This verse warns that no one should be sexually immoral or godless, like Esau. Someone who is sexually immoral lives in sexual sin. Someone who is godless treats what is sacred as having no value. Esau traded something very valuable for a single meal.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Christians who were weary and tempted to abandon their faith. He asks them to guard holiness and the grace of God. The story of Esau, found in Genesis 25, is a warning. Some believe that the sexual immorality mentioned in the verse also refers to Esau, but the biblical text does not say this clearly.

Today, we can ask ourselves what valuable things from God we are exchanging for a passing desire. Before giving in to a quick pleasure, it is wise to remember what truly matters and to ask God for strength to decide with wisdom.
exp.10:39:
God had planned something better for us, the believers who live after Christ. Because of this, the faithful of the Old Testament were not brought to their full goal apart from us. "Made perfect" means brought to completion or fulfillment. All of them will be made complete together.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were suffering and could be tempted to give up their faith. He has just recalled heroes who trusted God even though they endured hardship and did not see the promise fulfilled. Many understand that "something better" refers to Christ and his finished work, although the text does not spell this out.

Today, this reminds you that you do not walk alone. Your faith is part of a great story, with believers from every age. If you are slow to see answers, keep trusting: God works through a plan that includes all of his people.
exp.0:4:
The verse asks a question: to which of the angels did God ever say, "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father"? It also asks: "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son." The relationship described is a unique bond between Father and Son. The implied answer is: to none of them.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus is superior to the angels, who were held in great honor. He quotes Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14. The angels are servants of God; only Jesus is called Son in this full sense.

For today: you do not need intermediaries to draw near to God. Jesus, the Son, has already made the purification for your sins. Pray with confidence, and let his place of honor give you security.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that, because of God's promise, we can speak with confidence and without fear. The phrase "with confidence" means without doubting. A "helper" is someone who assists us and holds us up. We say that the Lord is our help and that we will not be afraid. We can even ask, "What can man do to me?"

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers who were facing pressure. He has just reminded them of the promise, "I will never leave you, nor forsake you." So he says "so": since God promises to be with them, they can answer with courage. The quotation at the end is from Psalm 118:6.

When you feel afraid of rejection, a threat, or what others think of you, repeat this truth in prayer: "The Lord is my helper." Then take the right step in front of you, trusting that God goes with you.
exp.3:5:
This verse says that the promise of entering God's rest is still open: it still remains for some to enter it. The first people who heard the good news, the people of Israel in the desert, did not enter because they disobeyed. "Since it remains" means "since it is still waiting to be received." "Heard the good news" means they were told the message of God's promise. "Disobedience" here means refusing to trust and to listen to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to give up. He quotes Psalm 95 and Genesis to show that God's rest did not end with that generation. He warns them not to repeat the mistake of their ancestors.

For today: if you feel that God speaks to you through his Word, do not put it off. Respond with trust and simple obedience, today, in something concrete.
exp.1:1:
The explanation says that the law, the message spoken through angels, was binding and valid. For that reason, every transgression (rebelling against God) and every disobedience received its just punishment. The word "binding" in the verse means firm and reliable, and "just punishment" means the consequence that was rightly deserved.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whom we cannot identify with certainty, writes to believers who were tempted to drift away from the faith. He refers to the law of Moses, which according to Jewish tradition was given with the mediation of angels (also mentioned in Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19). He argues that if ignoring that message had consequences, then ignoring the message of Christ, which is greater, is even more serious.

Today, let us not take lightly what God has said to us in Christ. Make time to read the Bible and to obey it, so that you do not slowly drift away without noticing.
exp.6:21:
This verse says that Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant. A guarantee is someone who takes responsibility and ensures that a promise will be kept. In this verse, "covenant" is the agreement God makes with his people. So Jesus is the sure guarantee of a covenant superior to the previous one.

The writer is the author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know with certainty. He speaks to believers of Jewish background who were tempted to return to the old ways. He has just shown that God swore that Jesus would be a priest forever, something that was not said of the Levitical priests. That oath of God is the basis of the guarantee: the covenant rests on a firm promise.

For today: when you doubt whether God will sustain you, remember that your relationship with him does not depend on your steadiness, but on Jesus, who lives forever and stands as guarantee for you. Rest in him and pray with confidence.
exp.5:2:
It says that the author and his readers are going to move on toward maturity in faith, and that they will do so "if God permits," that is, if God wills it. The word "perfection" here points to maturity, not to being without sin.

The author of Hebrews (we do not know for certain who he was) writes to believers who had grown stagnant. He encourages them to stop repeating the basics, such as repentance and faith, and to grow in the knowledge of Christ. With this phrase he acknowledges that everything depends on God. He then gives a serious warning about those who turn away, a passage that Christians interpret in various ways.

For today: make plans to grow spiritually, such as reading the Bible regularly and serving others, but with humility, depending on God and saying, "If God wills."
exp.6:22:
This verse says that under the old system there were many priests, one after another, because death prevented them from continuing to serve. In this verse, "since death prevented them" is the key idea, and "continuing in office" means remaining in the role of priest.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give and who has been much debated, writes to believers with a Jewish background who valued the Levitical priesthood. He wants to show them that Jesus is superior. The ancient priests died and had to be replaced, but Jesus, according to the next verse, lives forever and has a priesthood that does not pass to another.

For today: you can draw near to God with confidence, knowing that your priest never leaves and will never be replaced. When you feel weak or guilty, pray without fear, because Jesus lives always to intercede for you.
exp.8:25:
He says that if Christ's sacrifice had not been enough, he would have had to suffer again and again since the foundation of the world. But that was not the case: now, once for all at the end of the ages, Jesus has appeared and offered himself. "Doing away with sin" means removing it completely and putting an end to its power.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He compares Christ with the high priest, who entered the sanctuary every year with blood that was not his own. Christ, by contrast, entered heaven itself with his own sacrifice, made only once.

For today: if Christ has already dealt with sin once for all, you do not have to carry guilt trying to earn forgiveness. Draw near to God with confidence and gratitude, not with fear.
exp.11:4:
They say the readers have forgotten a word of encouragement that addresses them as sons. That word, taken from Proverbs 3:11-12, says: do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when he rebukes you. Here "discipline" means training and instruction, not only punishment for a fault. "Lose heart" means to give up in discouragement.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers worn down by opposition and trials. He asked them to look to Jesus, who endured hostility. Now he reminds them that suffering does not mean God has abandoned them. On the contrary, the following text explains that the Father disciplines those he loves as a parent does with a child.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not rush to think that God has rejected you. Pray sincerely and ask him what he wants to teach you, without giving up or hardening your heart. His fatherly care is still with you.
exp.8:2:
This verse describes the inner part of the tabernacle, the room that was behind a second curtain. The curtain that separated the two rooms is the veil, and the sacred room behind it, where the ark of the covenant stood, was called the Most Holy Place. Here the word "tabernacle" refers to that inner room of the tent of worship.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, writes to believers of Jewish background. He reminds them how worship was carried out under the first covenant, so that he can later show that Christ brings something better. First he describes in detail the place where God made His presence known.

Today we can be thankful that Jesus opened the way to God. What once lay behind a curtain, we can now approach in prayer with confidence, without depending on rituals or human mediators.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that we now see Jesus crowned with glory and honor. Before that, he was made "a little lower than the angels," meaning he took on human life for a time. He suffered death and, by the grace of God, tasted death for everyone, that is, he truly experienced it, on behalf of every person. "But" is the word that connects this part of the verse to what came before, and "suffering" refers to the pain he endured.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who needed encouragement. He has just quoted Psalm 8, which speaks of human beings placed over creation. He admits that we do not yet see everything made subject to them, but we do see Jesus, who passed through suffering before receiving glory.

For today: when you go through pain or trials, remember that Jesus knows suffering and lived through it out of love for you. Trust that God can lead your story toward hope, as He did with Him.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that Levi, the ancestor of the Jewish priests, was still within his ancestor Abraham when Abraham met Melchizedek. For this reason the verse speaks of Levi being "in the loin" of Abraham, which means that Levi was, in a certain sense, part of Abraham as one of his future descendants.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named and whose identity is uncertain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He wants to show that Jesus, a priest "after the order of Melchizedek," is greater than the Levitical priesthood. If Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek, then the descendants of Levi gave one too, and so Melchizedek is greater. It is an argument in the style of his time.

For today: we do not need another mediator to draw near to God. Jesus is our perfect and permanent priest. Today you can pray with confidence, without fear, because He represents you before the Father.
exp.8:19:
This verse records the words of Moses when he sealed the covenant at Sinai. "Covenant" here means a solemn agreement. The blood showed that this covenant was serious and came from God. "Which God has commanded you to keep" means that God had ordered the people to honor it.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers of Jewish background and recalls what happened in Exodus 24. Moses read the law to the people and sprinkled them with blood. He wants to show that even the first covenant did not begin without blood, and so he prepares the idea that the new covenant is sealed with the blood of Christ.

For today: God does not treat his covenant lightly. Today you can come to him with gratitude, knowing that Christ paid a very high price for you. That gratitude can lead you to keep your commitments to him with joy and to take them seriously.
exp.9:1:
If the sacrifices of the law could truly cleanse, would they not have stopped being offered? Those who worshipped, once they were fully cleansed, would no longer feel the guilt of their sins.

The author of Hebrews, who is not named in the text, is writing to believers with a Jewish background. He wants to show that the sacrifices repeated year after year were only a shadow, pointing to something greater. That they had to be repeated was a sign that they did not remove sin completely. This prepares the argument that Christ's sacrifice does, once for all.

Today: if you have trusted in Christ, do not carry a guilt that he has already carried. When you remember a sin, confess it honestly, but rest in his complete forgiveness, and live with gratitude rather than fear.
exp.1:12:
This verse contains two quotations from the Old Testament. Jesus says, "I will put my trust in him," meaning in God. He also says, "Here am I, and the children God has given me." The first phrase is usually related to Isaiah 8:17-18, though some understand these words differently. Here Jesus speaks as a man who trusts the Father and presents his own as his family. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers. Then the text explains that he became human to overcome death.

Today we can rest in this: Jesus knows our weakness because he lived it. When you feel alone or afraid, remember that you belong to his family. Trust God as Jesus did, and pray with the assurance that he is with you.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that Jesus speaks about God to his brothers and sisters. "I will proclaim Your name" means to make God's name known, and "Your name" stands for who God truly is. "The assembly" is the gathered community of believers, and "I will sing Your praises" means to sing or speak with gratitude and honor.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 22:22 and places these words on the lips of Christ. It follows from saying that Jesus is not ashamed to call those he makes holy "brothers." Many understand that Jesus, by becoming human and suffering, joins himself to his people and leads their worship. The psalm begins in anguish but ends in praise, and so it fits the theme of suffering that leads to glory.

Today you can remember that Jesus considers you part of his family and that, when you praise with other believers, you are not singing alone. Take part with joy in your church, and speak of how good God is with your family and friends.
exp.3:15:
Hebrews 4:16 invites us to draw near to God with confidence, without fear. The verse's call to approach with confidence means to come near, to draw close. "The throne of grace" is the place where God rules and offers his undeserved favor. There we receive mercy, meaning forgiveness and compassion, and we find grace, meaning help that arrives just when we most need it.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up. He reminds them that Jesus, called the high priest, faced trials just as we do, yet without sinning. For that reason he understands our weaknesses. Since Jesus is with the Father, we can draw near with assurance.

Today, when you feel weak, guilty, or under pressure, do not wait to get yourself together first. Pray sincerely and tell God what you are facing. He receives you with mercy and gives you help in your time of need.
exp.9:31:
Remember the early days that you were in the light. This verse invites readers to look back at the past. The words "you were in the light" refer to those who had come to know and receive the truth of Christ. After that moment, they endured a great conflict in the face of suffering, that is, a long and hard struggle with many hardships.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who are weary and tempted to abandon their faith. Earlier he had warned them firmly about the danger of turning away from God. Now he gently reminds them that they have already endured difficult trials, to encourage them not to give up.

For today: when you feel weary in the faith, remember how God sustained you in hard moments. Write down some of those experiences and thank Him for them. That remembrance can give you strength to keep trusting Him today.
exp.7:10:
In the new covenant, no one will need to teach their neighbor or their brother, "Know the Lord," because everyone will know him, from the least of them to the greatest. The word "neighbor" here refers to the people around us and those close to us in daily life.

The writer of Hebrews quotes the promise from Jeremiah 31:31-34. He writes to believers with a Jewish background, who were probably tempted to return to the old ways, in order to show them that Christ brings a better covenant. Here God speaks: he promises a personal knowledge of himself, one that comes from the law written on the heart and from the forgiveness of sins. Scholars debate how fully this has been fulfilled, whether it is already taking place or something is still to come.

For today: do not be content to know God only through what others tell you. Set aside time to speak with him and to read his Word, and keep encouraging others to grow.
exp.10:6:
By faith Noah believed the warning God gave him about something no one could yet see: the flood. Moved by godly fear, he built the ark to save his family. In the verse, the ark is what he built. His obedience stood in sharp contrast to the unbelief of others, which is why the verse says that by his faith he condemned the world. God counted him righteous because he trusted Him.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, encourages Christians to keep going in faith. Earlier he spoke of Enoch, who pleased God through faith. Now he offers Noah as another example, and right after this he will present Abraham, who also obeyed without seeing the whole path.

For today: trust God and obey Him, even when we do not yet see the result. Ask yourself what simple step of obedience God is asking of you, and take it today with reverence and confidence.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that God makes us holy, meaning he sets us apart for himself and cleanses us, through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ. He did it once for all, so it never needs to be repeated. "By that will" refers to God's plan, which Jesus came to carry out.

The author of Hebrews, whose identity is not known for certain, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He quotes Psalm 40 as the words of Christ: "Here I am, to do your will."
