He wants to show that the animal sacrifices, offered again and again every day, could not take away sins, but Jesus' sacrifice could.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through effort or carry guilt that has already been forgiven. When you fail, return to God with confidence, remembering that Christ's work is already complete, and live grateful, obeying him with joy.
exp.3:4:
This verse repeats a phrase from Psalm 95: "They shall never enter My rest." The author of Hebrews quotes it again to remind his readers that God spoke these words in earnest, as a warning. The word "rest" means peace and settled trust in God, a place where a person stops struggling on their own.

The author writes to believers who were in danger of growing weary or drifting away from the faith. He reminds them of what happened to the people of Israel in the wilderness: God offered them rest in the promised land, but many did not enter because of their disobedience and lack of trust. The author shows that this promise of rest remains open to those who believe.

Today we can ask ourselves where it is hard for us to trust God. Instead of hardening our hearts, we can obey his voice with simplicity and hand over our burdens, knowing that he invites us to rest in him.
exp.0:11:
God says that he will do with the heavens and the earth what is done with a worn-out robe: he will roll them up, and they will be changed. The phrases "roll them up" and "changed" are the ones to notice here. By contrast, the Son remains the same, and his years will never end.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 102 and applies it to the Son, that is, to Jesus. He wants to show his readers, believers of Jewish background who may have felt pressure to turn back, that Christ is superior to the angels. The angels serve, but the Son is eternal and created all things. Scholars agree that the central theme is the greatness of Christ.

Today, when everything changes, whether the news, our health, or our work, you can rest in someone who does not change. When you feel that something is wearing out or being lost, pray and give it to Jesus, and trust that his faithfulness lasts forever.
exp.5:13:
It says God promised Abraham, with an oath: "I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants." The Hebrew wording "blessing I will bless... multiplying I will multiply" is an expression that adds emphasis, meaning that it will certainly happen.

The author of Hebrews speaks to Christians who were growing weary in their faith. He asks them not to be slow or discouraged, and to imitate those who waited patiently. He points to God's promise to Abraham to show that God not only spoke but swore by himself. Abraham waited a long time, and the promise was fulfilled step by step.

For today: when you feel that God is taking a long time to answer, remember that his word is firm. You can keep trusting and waiting patiently, relying on what he has already promised in the Bible, even though you do not yet see the full result.
exp.1:17:
It says that Jesus suffered when he was tempted, and that is why he can help those who are going through temptation today. The word translated "suffered" means endured pain or hardship; "help" here means to come to someone's aid.

The author of Hebrews, whose name the letter does not mention, writes to believers from a Jewish background who needed encouragement not to abandon their faith. Earlier he explains that Jesus became human, sharing in our flesh and blood, so that he could be a merciful and faithful high priest. This verse completes that thought: Jesus understands our struggle because he lived through it.

For today: when you face temptation, do not hide or feel ashamed. Bring your weakness to Jesus in prayer, with confidence, knowing that he does not look on you with indifference but understands you and wants to help you.
exp.12:3:
Hebrews 13:4 says that marriage should be honored by all, and that the marriage bed should be kept undefiled. It also says that God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. The verse places marriage at a high level of respect and treats faithfulness within it as something pure and good, while warning that sexual immorality and infidelity will face God's judgment.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, closes his letter with practical instructions for Christian living. Earlier he speaks of hospitality and of caring for prisoners; afterward, of money and trust in God. In this setting, faithfulness in marriage appears as part of a life given over to God.

Today we can honor marriage by being faithful in our actions and thoughts, speaking respectfully of our spouse, and caring for mutual trust. If you are single, you can also honor marriage by living with purity and supporting the married couples around you.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that the good news was brought to us too, just as it was to the people of Israel in the wilderness. But hearing the message did not benefit them, because they did not share the faith of those who understood it. The phrase "the good news" refers to the message of God's promise. The phrase "did not share the faith" means they did not take hold of that message with real trust in God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were at risk of drifting away. He reminds them of the generation of the exodus, who heard God's promise about the land of rest but did not enter because of their unbelief. He warns them kindly not to repeat that mistake.

For today: hearing the Bible or attending church is not enough. Today you can choose one promise of God, trust it, and obey it in something concrete this week.
exp.1:4:
For it is not to angels that God has placed the world to come, which we are talking about. This means the new age that God will bring, the one the letter is describing. The angels were not given authority over it.

The author of Hebrews, who does not name himself and whom we cannot identify with certainty, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to let their faith grow weak. He has already shown that Jesus is greater than the angels. Now he makes clear that the future kingdom will not be handed over to them. Right after this, he quotes Psalm 8, which speaks of the human being crowned with glory, and he will apply it to Jesus.

For today: do not place your final trust in anything created, not even in impressive spiritual things. Fix your gaze on Jesus, who holds authority and invites you to persevere with firmness in your salvation.
exp.9:37:
The explanation says that the righteous one, that is, the person who is right with God, will live by trusting in Him. But if someone shrinks back, that is, turns away and abandons that trust, God takes no pleasure in that person. The phrase "I will take no pleasure in him" means that God does not find joy in such a person.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who are tired and pressed by difficulties. Here he quotes the prophet Habakkuk (2:3-4), where God speaks. He reminds them that they need patience, that Christ will return soon, and that they must not give up. Then he encourages them by saying that they are not among those who shrink back, but among those who persevere.

When you are tired of praying or of waiting for an answer, do not turn away from God. Take one simple step of trust today: pray, read a passage of the Bible, and tell Him that you still trust Him.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that when we go through correction or discipline, God treats us as his children. The phrase "endure suffering as discipline" in this reader's verse points to the idea of bearing hard things as training rather than seeing them as pointless, and "discipline" here means training and instruction rather than punishment for its own sake. The closing question is clear: no father who truly cares for his son goes without disciplining him.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers worn down by trials and encourages them by citing Proverbs 3:11-12. He reminds them that difficulties can be part of God's care. Not all suffering comes from correction for sin; the text speaks of the discipline that shapes character.

For today: when you go through a hard situation, instead of asking only "why me?", ask "what is God wanting to teach me?". Pray with humility, trust that He loves you, and let that trial draw you closer to Him rather than push you away.
exp.11:23:
Hebrews 12:24 says that believers have come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, the one who brings God and people together through that covenant. It also speaks of the sprinkled blood, the blood that was sprinkled, as was done in the sacrifices. That blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were tempted to give up. He contrasts Mount Sinai, a place of fear, with the heavenly city of God. The blood of Abel cried out for justice (Genesis 4:10); the blood of Jesus speaks of forgiveness and reconciliation.

Today, when guilt accuses you, remember that the blood of Jesus speaks a better word. Draw near to God with confidence, without fear, and listen to his voice.
exp.3:7:
It says that Joshua could not give the people true rest from God. If he had, God would not have spoken later about another day to enter that rest, in the words of Psalm 95. "Would have given them rest" means he would have brought them into complete rest. The name Joshua here refers to the leader who brought Israel into the promised land.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers tempted to abandon their faith. He reminds them that Israel entered Canaan, yet God, long afterward, still spoke of a rest yet to come. In this way he shows that the promise pointed to something deeper than a land: rest in God himself.

For today: do not look for lasting peace in achievements, places, or human help. When you are weary, listen today to the voice of God and trust in Christ, who offers a rest that nothing in this world can give.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that Moses was faithful in all that God entrusted to him, as a servant within the house of God. Here the verse's own wording stands in for the source phrases: the reader should understand "Now" as opening the sentence, and "was" as the verse's "was faithful." His service testified to what God would say later, that is, it pointed ahead to what would be spoken in the future.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known with certainty, writes to Christians from a Jewish background who faced pressure and temptation to abandon the faith. He honors Moses, but shows that Jesus is greater: Moses was a servant in God's house, and Christ is the Son over it. Many understand that what Moses testified to pointed toward Christ.

For today: faithfulness in what God entrusts to us has value, even when our role seems small. Serve with constancy, and keep your trust placed in Christ, who is greater than all.
exp.10:1:
The explanation says that believers of ancient times were commended by God because of their faith. "Being commended" means that God spoke well of them and approved them. "The ancients" are the faithful men and women of Israel's past.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background who were going through trials and could feel tempted to give up their faith. After explaining what faith is, he begins to show examples from the Old Testament, such as Abel, to encourage them to keep trusting God.

For today: what God values in us is not perfection or success, but trust in Him. Today you can choose a difficult situation and say to God simply, "I trust You in this," and take the next step by obeying Him.
exp.9:28:
This verse asks a pointed question: if someone who rejected the law of Moses faced death without mercy, how much more severe a punishment do you think they deserve if they trample on the Son of God? To "trample on" the Son of God means to step on him and treat him with contempt. To "profane the blood of the covenant" is to treat as common and worthless the blood of Jesus, which seals the new covenant and sets his people apart. To "insult the Spirit of grace" is to scorn the Spirit who offers forgiveness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to believers who were tempted to turn back under pressure and suffering. He warns them that deliberately abandoning Christ is very serious. Interpreters debate whether he is speaking of true believers who lose their salvation or of those who only professed faith.

Today, let us not take lightly what Christ has done. Let us value his sacrifice with gratitude, and if we drift away, let us return to him with humility and not with indifference.
exp.5:8:
He says that the author is confident that his readers, whom he calls "beloved," are in a better situation than those who fall away. The "better things" are good things that accompany salvation. The phrase "even though we speak like this" means: "even though I have just spoken to you with such harsh words."

The author of Hebrews, whose name the Bible does not give, has just issued a very serious warning about turning away from the faith. With the image of the land that bears fruit and the land full of thorns, he now softens his tone. He wants to shake them out of indifference, not discourage them. He sees real fruit in them: their service and their love for the saints.

For today: God's warnings are not meant to crush us, but to wake us up. Examine what fruits of love and service are in your life, and encourage someone in your church with words of trust and hope.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that whoever enters God's rest also stops working to earn his favor, just as God rested from his work when creation was finished. "Rest" here means peace, freedom from striving, and security in what God has already done. "Work" here refers to human efforts to deserve salvation.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were tempted to give up or turn back. He reminds them that Joshua led the people into the land, but not into the final rest. That rest is still open, and so he urges them not to harden their hearts like the generation in the wilderness.

For today: if you are tired from trying to be good enough before God, trust in what Christ has already done. Rest in his grace, and from there serve him with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.4:13:
The explanation says that solid food is for the mature, meaning those who, through constant practice, have trained their senses to tell good from evil. "Solid food" here means food for people who are fully grown and developed. "Constant use" refers to steady practice.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, lovingly rebukes believers who had already been in the faith for some time, yet still needed the basics, the milk. They ought to have been teachers, and yet they were stuck. He speaks to them this way to encourage them to grow.

For today: maturity does not come on its own with the years, but through practice. Read the Bible regularly and apply what you learn to concrete decisions. In this way your judgment is sharpened little by little, and you will be better able to discern what pleases God.
exp.12:17:
He says the author asks his readers to pray for him and for those who are with him. He states that they are convinced they have a clear conscience, that is, they do not feel they are acting with bad intentions. Moreover, they desire to live honorably in every way, meaning to live and behave in a right, upright manner in every area of life.

The author of Hebrews does not identify himself in the letter, and we do not know for certain who he was. He writes to a Christian community that he knows and wants to visit again, as the following verse indicates. After speaking about obeying the leaders, he now places himself as someone who needs prayer. His request shows humility: even teachers depend on the prayers of others.

For today: pray specifically for your pastors, teachers, or leaders, that they may live with integrity. And examine your own conscience: ask God to help you live honestly in your everyday life.
exp.1:6:
It says that God made human beings a little lower than the angels, yet He honored them in a special way. The words "You crowned him" express the same idea, and the phrase about setting him over the works of God's hands carries the sense of putting him in charge. In other words, God gave humanity dignity and entrusted it with caring for what He created.

The writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 8, written by David. He wants to show that the world to come is not placed under the angels, but under human beings. Yet we do not yet see everything subject to humanity. That is why he points to Jesus: being a man, He was made lower for a time, suffered death for everyone, and was crowned with glory. Many understand the text to speak of humanity and of Jesus as its head.

For today: your life has a worth that God Himself gave. When you feel small or unimportant, remember that God sees you, honors you, and has entrusted you with responsibilities. Take care of them with gratitude.
exp.5:16:
God wanted to make it very clear to the heirs of the promise that his purpose does not change, so he guaranteed it with an oath. This is the point of the verse: God's plan is unchanging, and he chose to confirm it in a way that gives his people solid assurance.

The author of Hebrews writes to believers who are weary and tempted to give up. He has just spoken of Abraham, who waited patiently and received the promise. Just as people swear an oath to settle a matter, God also made an oath. He did not do this because his word was weak, but to give us greater assurance. The "heirs" are those who trust God as Abraham did.

When you doubt or when the waiting grows long, remember that God not only promised but also bound himself with an oath. You can rest your hope on his faithful character, and pray with confidence, even when you do not see quick answers.
exp.8:5:
When everything had been prepared in this way, the priests entered regularly into the first room to perform their sacred duties. The verse describes a daily routine: with the furnishings of the tabernacle set in place, the priests went into the first room, called the Holy Place, to carry out their work of worship. Their sacred duties were the everyday religious tasks, such as offering incense and tending the lamps and the bread.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to believers of Jewish background. He describes the tabernacle to show that this system had limits. The priests entered one room, but only the high priest, once a year, entered the innermost room. All of this pointed toward Christ opening a better way.

Today we can draw near to God without human go-betweens or repeated rituals, because Jesus has already opened the way. Pray with confidence and gratitude, knowing that God receives you because of what Christ has done.
exp.6:18:
The explanation says that the law of Moses could not bring anyone to perfection, that is, to a full and complete relationship with God. But now a better hope has been introduced, and through it we are able to draw near to God. The explanation also points out a detail in the wording: the idea of drawing near in this verse is the same idea as drawing near to God.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not given in the text, writes to believers with a Jewish background. He explains that Jesus is a priest forever, in the manner of Melchizedek, and not according to the Levitical priesthood. For this reason the old commandment about the priesthood is set aside: it was weak and unable to give full access to God. That better hope is Christ himself.

Today you can draw near to God without depending on your merits or your performance. When you feel that you do not measure up, pray with confidence, remembering that Jesus, your priest, has already opened the way to God.
exp.10:38:
These were all commended by God for their faith, meaning God saw their trust and was pleased with them. Yet even so, they did not live to receive what had been promised. The promise would be fully realized in Christ and his salvation.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish believers who were suffering and might feel like giving up their faith. He reminds them of faithful people from the Old Testament who trusted God without seeing everything fulfilled. The following verse explains that God had something better prepared for all of them together.

For today: if you are still waiting for an answer from God, do not think that he has forgotten you. You can keep trusting, because faith does not depend on seeing everything fulfilled now, but on believing that God is faithful.
exp.9:33:
The verse says that the believers to whom this was written shared the suffering of those in prison: the phrase "sympathized with those in prison" means that they felt the pain of those who were locked up as if it were their own. They also joyfully accepted the confiscation of their property. Their joy came from knowing that they themselves had a better and permanent possession, a treasure more valuable and lasting in heaven.

The author of Hebrews, whose name is not known for certain, writes to Jewish Christians who were going through hardships. He reminds them how brave they were at the beginning of their faith, to encourage them not to give up now and to keep their confidence until the end.

Today we can ask ourselves what we value most. When we place our security in what is eternal, it will be easier to be generous, to stand with those who suffer, and to bear losses with hope.
exp.11:3:
It says that the readers have not yet reached the point of resisting to the point of shedding their blood, that is, to the point of death, in their struggle against sin. "Not yet" means "not yet." "Struggle" speaks of fighting with firmness.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to Christians who are tired from pressure and suffering. He has just presented Jesus as an example of endurance to the cross. Now he reminds them with affection that, although their struggle is hard, they have not reached the extreme that Jesus lived. Many think that "sin" here includes the temptation to give up and abandon the faith, but the text does not spell this out.

For today: when you feel worn out from struggling against a temptation or from staying faithful, look to Jesus and remember that he already walked a much harder road. Ask him for strength today and take one more step, without losing heart.
exp.9:30:
It says that falling into the hands of the living God is a terrible thing, one that brings great fear. The word for "fearful" means frightening or worthy of fear, and "falling into his hands" means facing his judgment. "The living God" reminds us that God is real, active, and sees everything.

The author of Hebrews, whose name we do not know for certain, writes to tired Jewish Christians who were tempted to turn back. He warns them that deliberately abandoning Christ and despising his sacrifice is very serious. He cites the Old Testament to remind them that God judges his people. Then, in the verses that follow, he encourages them to remember their faithfulness in the past.

For today: do not take God's grace lightly. Let your trust in Christ be sincere, and let reverent fear lead you to persevere, not to live in dread, because in Jesus we have secure access to God.

sum.10: Hebrews 11 explains that faith means trusting what God promises even when it cannot yet be seen, and that without faith it is impossible to please God. It recalls Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and many others, who trusted and obeyed even while suffering. All of them looked forward to something better, and God had prepared something better for us as well.
sum.5: The author encourages believers to move on toward maturity and seriously warns about those who receive great blessings and then turn away. He is confident that his readers will bear better fruit, and he asks them to persevere in faith and patience, as Abraham did. God's promise, affirmed with an oath, is a firm anchor for the soul, and Jesus has already entered on our behalf.
sum.7: Hebrews 8 teaches that Jesus is our High Priest, seated at the right hand of God and serving in the true sanctuary in heaven. His ministry is better because he is the mediator of a new covenant with better promises. Under it, God writes his law on the heart, everyone knows him, and he forgives sins forever.
sum.3: Hebrews 4 warns us that the promise of entering God's rest still stands, but we must receive it with faith and obedience, so that we do not fall short the way those did who refused to obey. God's word is living and powerful, cutting deeper than any sword, and it sees everything in our hearts. Jesus, our great High Priest, understands our weaknesses, so we can approach his throne of grace with confidence.
sum.11: Hebrews 12 encourages us to run the race of faith with patience, keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross. God corrects us as a loving Father would, so that we may produce the fruit of righteousness, and He calls us to pursue peace and holiness. We have come to Mount Zion, so we should serve God with reverence.
sum.12: Hebrews 13 calls believers to live out their faith in everyday life: to love one another as brothers and sisters, to be welcoming to strangers, to remember those in prison, to honor marriage, and to be content without greed, because God will never abandon them. It asks them to follow Jesus, who does not change, and to obey their leaders. It ends with a blessing, asking that God would equip them to do his will.
sum.8: Hebrews 9 describes the tabernacle of the first covenant and the sacrifices that were repeated year after year, yet could not cleanse the conscience. Christ entered once and for all into heaven itself with his own blood and obtained eternal redemption. One day he will return, without sin, to save those who are waiting for him.
sum.2: Hebrews 3 invites us to fix our eyes on Jesus, who is faithful and greater than Moses. Moses was a servant in God's house, but Christ is the Son who is over it. It recalls how the Israelites, because of their unbelief and disobedience in the wilderness, did not enter God's rest, and so it encourages us not to harden our hearts, but to encourage one another every day and remain steadfast.
sum.9: Hebrews 10 teaches that the sacrifices under the law could not take away sin, but Jesus Christ, with one offering of his body, cleansed us and made us holy forever. Because of this, we can approach God with confidence, hold firmly to our faith, encourage one another, and not give up meeting with the congregation. The text warns against rejecting Christ and calls for steadfast endurance with patience.
sum.4: Hebrews 5 explains that every high priest is chosen from among men and is weak like them, and he does not give himself this honor but is called by God. Christ was called by God, learned obedience through suffering, and became the source of eternal salvation for those who obey him. The author rebukes his readers because they still act like children who need milk and must grow up.
sum.6: Hebrews 7 explains that Melchizedek, king of righteousness and of peace, blessed Abraham and received his tithes, which shows that his priesthood is greater than that of Levi. Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, is a priest forever according to that order, with God's oath. He lives always to intercede, and he offered himself once for all, so he brings us near to God and saves completely.
sum.1: Hebrews 2 calls us to pay close attention to the great salvation that God confirmed with signs and miracles. Jesus became human, made a little lower than the angels, and suffered death for everyone. In this way he defeated the power of the devil, freed people from the fear of death, and is able to help those who are being tempted.
sum.0: God spoke long ago through the prophets, but now he has spoken to us through his Son. He made the Son heir of all things and created the universe through him. The Son reflects God's glory, sustains all things, has cleansed our sins, and sits at the right hand of God. For this reason he is greater than the angels, who are servants sent to help those who will inherit salvation.
